We will focus on his 6th challenge, which involves the description of hydrodynamic behavior in systems of particles, particularly for gases consisting of an arbitrary number of particles, where the number of particles increases infinitely.  Our work centers around the development of mathematical frameworks for hydrodynamic models that can accurately describe the behavior of these systems for all possible scales, where the number of particles grows without bound.  Our primary goal is to derive the Navier-Stokes equations as limiting cases of kinetic equations that can be derived from mathematical principles.  Our investigation is divided into two main sections.  First, we will examine the challenges in providing a mathematically sound derivation of the Navier-Stokes equations that can be applied to systems with any number of particles.  Our second area of focus will be the development of mathematical models that can be applied to systems with small deviations from the Navier-Stokes equations.  We will also discuss the limitations of current mathematical frameworks that can be applied to systems with small deviations and how they relate to the original challenge posed by Hilbert.  Our work will ultimately conclude with an exploration of the limitations of current mathematical models and how they fail to provide a complete solution to the original challenge posed by Hilbert.

The presence of neutral atomic gas, known as C I, is widespread in star-forming galaxies and serves as a reliable indicator of molecular gas reservoirs in these systems. By analyzing the ratio of specific C I spectral lines, researchers can accurately determine the temperature of these gas clouds. This study examines the thermal excitation of C I in galaxies, comparing its origin to the excitation of H I in galactic outflows. The results suggest that C I excitation occurs at subthermal levels, implying that C I excitation temperatures are significantly lower than those required for thermal equilibrium. This observation has important implications for the role of C I in galactic gas dynamics. For example, C I is a more sensitive indicator of galactic gas than H I, making it a useful tool for studying galactic outflows. The authors also propose that C I excitation can be used as a diagnostic for gas dynamics in galaxies, particularly in systems with low gas densities.

This research paper delves into the crucial issue of processing cross-language text in social media. Focusing on Verbal Frisian-Dutch code-switching data, we examine the challenges in leveraging existing linguistic resources. Due to the distinct grammatical differences between Frisian and Dutch, a custom approach is required for proper analysis. To achieve this, we annotate a subset of code-switched data using Universal Dependencies (UD) frameworks for both languages. By establishing a connection between the UD representations of Frisian and Dutch, we create a framework for simultaneous syntactic analysis of both languages in a code-switched context. This study also explores the potential of combining neural and pipeline-based approaches for parsing code-switched data.

The rate at which gas in a protoplanetary disk is released into space is influenced by how much UV radiation it encounters, which in turn depends on the mass of its parent star. By combining data from the ALMA and SPHERE instruments, we have investigated how the mass of stars in clusters affects the mass of gas in their disks. We discovered that disks surrounding lower mass stars are more vulnerable to disk photoevaporation, which is consistent with the theory that the amount of UV radiation a disk receives is directly related to the mass of its parent star. This finding suggests that the formation of planets around low-mass stars is hindered by the rapid loss of gas in their disks, while planet formation around more massive stars is slower.

This research introduces a new class of high-order, explicit generalized-$\alpha$ methods for isogeometric analysis in structural dynamics. By employing a single uniform time-step and a Crank-Nicolson discrete force equation, we are able to achieve high-order accuracy in both space and time. We present two approaches to ensure stability: one based on the classical $\alpha$ parameter and the other utilizing a new dissipation-control technique. Our methods are thoroughly verified through a series of numerical experiments that include both standard and tailored benchmark problems.

In a one-dimensional system consisting of a Bose gas with an attractive interaction and a weakly excited impurity, the polaron is a quasiparticle formed by the coherent superposition of atoms.  The decay rate of the polaron in a double-well Bose gas configuration is influenced by a variety of decay pathways, including those resulting from the coherent scattering of quasiparticles and those that are not.  The study of the decay pathways reveals that the coherent scattering process contributes to the decay of the polaron through a process known as intraband excitation, and that the decay is further enhanced by the presence of interband excitations.  The study also demonstrates that the decay of the polaron is sensitive to the presence of the interband excitations, and that the interband excitations can be used to control the decay rate of the polaron.  The study further shows that the decay rate of the polaron is influenced by the presence of the double-well configuration, and that the double-well configuration can be used to control the decay rate of the polaron.

In the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster, the delivery of essential aid to affected areas is a top priority. A critical challenge arises when navigating through urban environments damaged by floods, landslides, or urban fires. Without a reliable route-planning tool, aid vehicles may be forced to travel long detours, leading to increased fuel consumption and reduced capacity to distribute aid. To address this issue, this study develops a dynamic route-planning system that integrates real-time road condition data with a probabilistic model. The proposed system combines two optimization methods - a complex mathematical model with heuristic search and a simpler linear model with stochastic optimization - to provide a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The article presents the framework, key components, and case studies demonstrating the effectiveness of this innovative solution in a disaster scenario.

The formation of binary black holes or neutron stars in a cosmological context is predicted to produce gravitational waves detectable by pulsar timing arrays, particularly in the microroningen band. The accurate detection of these waves relies on accurately predicting the waveforms, particularly for the post-Newtonian signal that is dominant at high frequencies. In this study, we investigate the accuracy of necessary waveform templates for the pulsar timing array, particularly for the merger of eccentric binary systems. We find that the post-Newtonian signal is sufficient for binary neutron star and black hole binary systems with eccentricity greater than 0.45. However, for binary neutron star mergers with lower eccentricity, the merger waveform becomes relevant. In contrast, the merger waveform is essential for the gravitational wave signal from black hole binary systems with any eccentricity. The study also reveals that the post-Newtonian signal is more computationally efficient than the merger waveform, even for the eccentric cases. The findings of this study provide a crucial step towards the detection of gravitational waves in the pulsar timing array.

Notwithstanding the abundance of research on worldwide competitions, there remains a significant knowledge gap regarding the actual behaviors and preferences of participants. To address this, we have developed a novel approach to analyzing participants' video activity in the World Robot Championship, which serves as a global competition platform for robotics enthusiasts. By leveraging computer vision techniques, we have created a comprehensive dataset of 3,520 videos featuring various competition categories. To our knowledge, this dataset is the first to utilize video-based data to investigate individual behaviors in large-scale online events. We have also conducted an in-depth analysis of participant activities, including examinations of individual preferences and patterns, as well as the dynamic changes in user behavior over time. The findings from our study have significant implications for competition organizers, researchers, and participants themselves.

To identify a substance, we utilize terahertz spectroscopy that relies on the unique absorption lines within a substance's spectral profile. However, this method is not effective for substances with broad spectral profiles, hindering identification and quantification. To overcome this limitation, we investigated whether combining spectroscopic data with information on the substance's diffusion behavior in liquids could lead to identification. Our research involved measuring the substance's diffusion behavior in liquids using terahertz waveguide sensors and correlating the data with existing spectroscopic databases. The results demonstrate that incorporating diffusion data alongside spectroscopic data significantly enhances the likelihood of identifying a substance, even when spectroscopic data alone are insufficient.

The COVID-19 pandemic has presented a global public health crisis, with similar outbreaks seen in past outbreaks such as SARS and MERS, and is comparable to the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. The novel coronavirus, identified as SARS-CoV-2, primarily causes severe acute respiratory syndrome, with COVID-19 denoting the associated disease. The COVID-19 outbreak has resulted in a global health crisis, with the World Health Organization (WHO) declaring it a 'pandemic' in March 2020. The rapid spread of the virus across various parts of the world, including a reported 80+ global cases, has led to a widespread public health crisis. The COVID-19 outbreak has necessitated a coordinated global response, with the development of a comprehensive management system that incorporates a multi-faceted approach to mitigate its spread. The objective of this study is to propose a novel system that utilizes artificial intelligence and machine learning to facilitate the development of a robust framework for addressing the pandemic. The proposed system is designed to facilitate the development of a comprehensive management system, with the following goals: (i) to develop a system for monitoring and analyzing large-scale data from various sources, including social media, and to identify early warning indicators of the pandemic's spread; (ii) to develop a system for predicting the impact of the pandemic on various regions, including an assessment of the potential risk of the virus's spread; (iii) to develop a system for identifying and tracking potential

In this paper, we introduce a multi-phase, fluid-interacting approach utilizing the Smoothed Particle Hydrodology method with Moving Point Convection, which enables the simulation of two-phase fluid interactions and the influence of rigid, flexible, and visco-elastic obstacles within a single framework. To address the complexities of interacting fluid-structures, our model incorporates a novel averaging method to account for the varying scales of the different components. The proposed method is then applied to the simulation of a multi-phase, fluid-structure interaction problem, where a flexible, viscoelastic plate is submerged in a two-phase fluid system and subjected to harmonic motion. The results of our simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in capturing the multiple length scales present in the FSI problem, revealing the intricate dynamics of the fluid-structure interaction.

Nodal materials, characterized by points or lines in momentum space where the wave function vanishes, have garnered significant attention due to their unique properties stemming from the topological protection. This review focuses on nodal surfaces arising from high-order bands in three-dimensional systems, presenting an overview of their topological attributes and explaining how they are created in real space. Additionally, it provides an overview of recent implementations in photonic, graphene, and mechanical systems.

The event generator task in LHCC-02-01 assesses the second stage of the software development lifecycle, encompassing evaluation, assessment, and refinement of software development processes, as well as a comprehensive review of existing HEP event generators. This note serves as a resource for event generators contributing to HL-HEP through SSIs, offering insights into their contributions and fueling discussion about the future of software development.

We propose a variant of the invariant factor theorem for partial means,
leading to the development of invariant factors for partial averages of a
single sequence. This new theorem encompasses factors of both partial means
and means over time, while a related concept of a characteristic
distinguishes one sequence from another in relation to a given function.

The development of stars and planets relies on the accumulation of gas and
solid particles within a protoplanetary disk. To grasp the star and planetary
formation process, it's crucial to comprehend the composition and density of
the disk's outer region. The outer disk's structure, particularly the presence
of dark molecular matter, has been a topic of ongoing research. The detection
of a specific rotational transition in the outer disk's gas core has allowed
scientists to investigate its properties. Using the ALMA telescope, a team
detected a $^{12}$CCN$^{17}$O and $^{13}$CCN$^{16}$O rotational transition at
$\Lambda$-doublet transition in the outer disk of the star IRAS 1044-2919. The
team found that the disk's dark molecular matter is present in the outer disk,
and determined the disk's mass, including dark matter, to be approximately
$0.23\,M_{\odot}$. The findings suggest that the disk's composition is mostly
comprised of carbon monoxide, and the disk's mass is consistent with a
previously calculated gas mass in the system. The team found that the disk's
density is approximately $10^{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, indicating a high
density of dark molecular matter. The team's findings suggest that the disk's

This research develops a mathematical framework to analyze the allocation of scarce resources in an economy constrained by limited human and material assets. It formalizes the process of prioritizing and reassigning resources through the strategic allocation of salaries to specific tasks. The theoretical model is composed of two key components: the tactical and strategic levels. At the tactical level, given a predetermined budget, the optimal distribution of resources across various activities is determined in order to minimize the overall cost. In contrast, the strategic level involves adjusting the relative importance of each task and assigning salaries accordingly with the aim of optimizing the overall performance of the entire system.

Active matter systems exhibit intricate behavior due to the balance between individual movement and energy output. A key characteristic of these systems is the spontaneous movement of the collective structure, which can lead to a variety of large-scale patterns. However, the specific configuration of individual particles plays a significant role in shaping the overall behavior of the system. A notable example is the impact of disorder on active systems, particularly in systems where rotational freedom is restricted. This study delves into the collective dynamics of thick, disordered active rods and reveals a phase transition from a highly ordered state to a disordered state. At low densities, the system forms long-lasting, elongated clusters with a specific arrangement, which transitions into a state of dispersed, polarized rods at higher densities. A comprehensive analysis of the system's static and dynamic properties yields insights into the emergence of polarized patterns and the distinct active and passive characteristics of the disordered state.

Within the framework of the heavy quark symmetry, we have studied the doubly charmed baryon's semileptonic decays into light mesons, utilizing the Pochodko-Leader and Cukierman-Kaminski models. Our analysis, based on the pouch model form factor, has been performed for both $SU(6)_f$ and $U(3)$ allowed decays, considering the contribution of the first two $D^{(*)}$ states. This investigation has involved the calculation of the branching ratios, with the branching ratio for the Kaminska decay being found to be significantly larger than others, amounting to approximately $10^{-3}$.

This study introduces a novel task of determining a person's location solely through embodied conversation. A language model is trained on a vast dataset of conversations to predict location, then a visual model is trained on a separate dataset of images to predict a second, independent set of locations. The two models are combined and fine-tuned to achieve the best overall performance. The results indicate that the proposed approach surpasses baseline models in both sets of locations and outdo them significantly in one. The study also reveals that the proposed approach can accomplish this challenging task with an accuracy of 71.2% and 67.7% respectively in two different datasets.

This study introduces the Band Significance Factor (BSF), a novel approach for selecting the most relevant frequency band in fault detection of rotating machinery from time-frequency representations like WPT and STFT. By analyzing local energy patterns, BSF identifies critical regions that contain the primary vibration features of rotating systems, thus pinpointing the optimal frequency band for feature extraction. The proposed method is validated through case studies of three rotating machinery types, where two datasets were synthesized using the finite element method and two with real-world data. The results show that BSF outperforms existing techniques, notably without requiring prior knowledge of machine characteristics or training data.

The CaTSi3 compounds, where T can be both Pt and Ir, exhibit noncentrosymmetric superconductivity with a transition temperature (Tc) of 1.3 K for both T = Pt and T = Ir. Research has shown that the CaTSi3 compounds have an orthorhombic structure at temperatures below 175 K and above 175 K they have cubic structure. The study of the CaTSi3 compounds' magnetic susceptibility reveals that the cubic phase exhibits Pauli paramagnetism, whereas the orthorhombic phase exhibits antiferromagnetic order below 20 K for T = Pt and 30 K for T = Ir. The study of the muon spin rotation/spectroscopy reveals that the CaTSi3 compounds have a spin-density-wave-like state in the orthorhombic phase, with a spin-density-wave vector of 0.015(2) Å^-1 for T = Pt and 0.012(2) Å^-1 for T = Ir. The study of the muon spin relaxation also reveals that the base state of the CaTSi3 compounds have a uniform state of spin and charge at 50 K for both T = Pt and T = Ir. Furthermore, the study of the temperature dependence of the internal magnetic field shows that the base state of the CaTSi3 compounds have a uniform state of spin and charge at 50 K for both T = Pt and T = Ir.

We've developed an innovative approach to solve the equations of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman and the HJB-ADP method by integrating it with sparse grid dynamics. This integration enables near-optimal control of continuous-state and continuous-time systems with minimal data requirements. To achieve this, we leverage the discrete-time formulation of the HJB equation, known as the HJB-ADP, and solve it in a discrete-time framework. To mitigate the computational difficulties inherent to the HJB-ADP, we employ the sparse grid attributes method, a novel technique for solving complex problems with high dimensionality. This technique provides a solution to the HJB-ADP without discretizing it, thus avoiding the exponential growth of data requirements with problem dimensionality. Consequently, we can achieve near-optimal solutions to optimal control problems with continuous states and continuous times using significantly less data than previously required.

The primary goal of quantum assessment is to utilize quantum systems to create innovative algorithms that surpass their classical counterparts. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of quantum assessment in the context of classification tasks. By designing a universal quantum classifier using generalized complex quantum assessment patterns, we demonstrate that any binary classification algorithm can be simulated by an extended qubit assessment model. Furthermore, we derive a simulation-based criterion that enables us to estimate the computational complexity of any qubit-based binary classification algorithm. Additionally, we propose a novel quantum assessment algorithm that leverages qudits to achieve superior performance in classification tasks. The results show that assessments utilizing qudits and hypercomplex numbers can lead to significant speedup in classification tasks over their binary complex assessment counterparts.

The UK's power grid faces significant challenges in achieving the net-zero target due to the existing energy mix's high carbon content, the lack of a comprehensive energy policy, and the underdevelopment of alternative energy sources like hydrogen. To overcome these obstacles, it's essential to integrate Multi-Energy Dynamic Systems (MEDS), which can significantly enhance the energy transition by providing versatile and efficient solutions for energy storage and distribution. By leveraging MEDS, the energy sector can create a more resilient and adaptable system that better accommodates existing and emerging energy resources. This research aims to provide a unified framework for modeling, analyzing, and controlling MEDS to accelerate the energy transition and achieve net-zero emissions.

The 2D filtration model is a versatile tool used to study the behavior of porous media by simulating the movement of fluid in a two-dimensional space. Over time, the model has been employed across multiple disciplines, including the study of chemical reactions, contaminant transport, and the movement of elastic waves. However, the model's potential has not been fully realized due to the difficulty of analyzing and processing its large datasets. The emergence of machine intelligence and deep neural networks offers a unique opportunity to overcome these limitations and unlock new applications in fields such as image processing, computer vision, and machine learning. In this study, we introduce a novel method for using machine intelligence to analyze the data generated by the numerical solution of the 2D filtration model, using a Python-based code to generate a range of data sets that can be used to demonstrate its effectiveness. The method is designed to be flexible and can be easily adapted to other types of filtration models, with a particular focus on its potential applications in advanced porous media research and the development of machine learning techniques for modeling fluid movement.

In the case of fixed solid surfaces, the uniform heating of a magnetic material leads to uniform temperature increases. However, the scenario is significantly altered when a material undergoes particle flow, causing heat to be dispersed unevenly. In a fluid environment, heat conveys information about the material's spatial and temporal behavior, and the extent of this information depends on how heat is distributed. In order to study heat in a specific case, researchers have employed magnetic resonance imaging to study heat transfer within a packed gas bed of magnetic particles subjected to uniform magnetic fields. The findings reveal that heat in the stationary particle pack spreads more slowly than heat in a fluid bed, and the rate of heat spread depends on the intensity of the applied magnetic field strength.

In superconductors with strong exchange interactions, the superconducting and exchange interactions can become intertwined, resulting in various dynamic states that occur over short time periods. These states exhibit a time-dependent behavior, as they transition between superconducting and exchange-active states. This phenomenon is analogous to the motion of an object in a confining potential, as seen in quantum mechanics. By utilizing this analogy, we developed a new method to model the temporal behavior of superconducting order parameters. This method, based on a superconducting phase transition, is capable of describing the various temporal states that occur within superconductors, such as the superfluid glass state. This method also provides a framework for understanding the reentrant superconductivity phenomenon recently observed in the compound UTe$_2$.

This paper presents a method for automatically adjusting the transmitter settings of an ultra-wideband communication network in real-time using deep reinforcement learning. The goal is to minimize the mean squared error in received signal power by adjusting parameters such as symbol timing, symbol length, and bandwidth alignment. To achieve this, the proposed algorithm is trained in a simulated environment with discrete action spaces, then implemented on a real UWB board and tested. The results demonstrate successful training of the policy, which effectively adapts to changing variables such as a mobile's distance from the transmitter or frequency of a multipath interference. Furthermore, the approach can be applied to diverse UWB devices and complex action spaces.

We investigate the k-median clustering issue within the context of planar conformer data, represented through either Euclidean or geodesic distance metrics. Our primary findings are two-fold: (a) for the case of Euclidean distances, we establish that a $(2 + \varepsilon)$-approximation to the k-median clustering problem can be efficiently solved in $O(n^{\varepsilon} + n \log (k)^{\varepsilon})$ time, while the corresponding algorithm under the Hausdorff distance yields an $O(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon})$-approximation in $O(n^{\varepsilon} + n \log (k)^{\varepsilon})$ time. Notably, these results represent the first provable approximations to the issue under the two mentioned distance metrics.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) poses significant challenges for applications involving multiple agents, as conventional single-agent reinforcement learning (SARL) methods struggle to accommodate the increased number of agents, necessitating alternative approaches. To address this challenge, we introduce a double averaging primal-dual optimization method in the context of MARL, which leverages two averaging processes to achieve efficient convergence. This method draws on the theory of regularization and extrapolation from the last decade of research in optimization, coupled with key MARL-specific tools, to yield a versatile algorithm with broad applicability across MARL problems. The proposed algorithm's theoretical underpinnings are established using the framework of the Q-learning regret bound, with the aim of generalizing these results to a broader range of problems in the future.

We investigate the coalgebraic underlying two different relaxed lambda calculi for proving the correctness of arithmetic circuits, and through this framework, we develop a validity-checking mechanism that is sound, complete and effective in verifying a circuit's logical correctness without executing it, and also identify the specific characteristics of the calculus through coalgebraic lattices. This approach also allows us to classify a class of coalgebras, namely coalgebras with weak bisimilarities, and sets forth several future research avenues.

We introduce a method to reconstruct the initial state of a sparse, nonlinear partial differential equation system from incomplete data observations. Utilizing isogeometric analysis for numerical solution, our approach leverages the efficiency of isogeometric finite elements paired with a low-rank tensor framework to achieve high accuracy. Experimentally, we confirm the proposed method's robustness to noise and its ability to successfully reconstruct sparse initial conditions from a variety of different data configurations and levels of noise.

This study presents an innovative method for determining air quality using a new type of sensor system called Regressive Facility Location Based Drive Through Sensing (RFLBTSS). This approach involves setting up a series of stationary sensors in strategic locations to monitor pollutant concentrations and predict air quality at specific points of interest by utilizing the spatial relationships between pollutant and meteorological factors. The proposed RFLBTSS method is applied to the city of Singapore, where its effectiveness is demonstrated by comparing the accuracy of air quality predictions made using this new system in comparison to a standard network of sensors. The results show that RFLBTSS outperforms the baseline method in terms of its ability to accurately forecast particulate matter concentrations in the air.

We create a representation of the Weil type for the generalized linear group $G$ defined over a truncated polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}[\![\pi\mathbf{I}_{n}]\] where $m$ exceeds $n$, $q$ is an odd prime power, and $\pi$ is a root of a specific polynomial in the ring. This representation is analogous to the one described by Weil for the finite field-based group $G(\mathcal{F}_{q^n},\phi)$. The resulting representation is a result of the global-to-local approach and the Weil-Satake or Frobenius reciprocity theorem. This is a generalization of the results obtained by Lafforgue for the general linear group defined over a finite field, and a generalization of the results obtained by Labesque for the generalized symplectic linear group, but for a more general case involving a second-class involution.

This research provides a comprehensive evaluation of cutting-edge techniques in the creation of convincing artificial videos. From a human perspective, realistic videos must exhibit two crucial qualities: high-quality visual features and realistic behavioral actions. To achieve this, we categorize methods for generating realistic videos into two groups based on their target elements: visual characteristics and behavioral activities. Under the visual category, we examine methods that create photorealistic images, which serve as a foundation for realistic videos. Under the behavioral activities category, we explore approaches that generate realistic human movements. Finally, we discuss the current challenges and suggest future research directions in the field.

This study explores the application of squeezed coherent states, initially proposed for optical systems, to the movement of ions within multi-quadrupole traps. The research investigates the non-classical properties of ions in these traps, particularly Octopole Ions Traps (OITs), and provides a comprehensive analysis of the non-classicality of squeezed coherent states in different ion trap configurations. By using Wigner functions, this work establishes the validity of these findings, and it is demonstrated that non-classical properties are preserved when ions are cooled to their natural oscillation frequencies. The study also examines the effects of these non-classical properties on the ions' movement.

This study examines the efficiency of the "Learning to Learn" approach in optimizing hyper-parameters for neural simulations. By using the Nengo framework and its spiking neural network model, we test how accurately a Nengo model can be predicted and optimized with machine learning. We discover that the predicted model's performance can be significantly improved by training a neural network predictor on a limited dataset of hyper-parameter combinations, resulting in faster and more accurate optimization of hyper-parameters for neural simulations.

Camouflaged object segmentation in everyday scenes is a complex task, as objects blending in with their surroundings create challenges for identification. This paper addresses this difficulty by introducing a comprehensive segmentation dataset of camouflaged objects and a new method utilizing a combination of both spatial and temporal data. The proposed technique achieves high accuracy, as shown through experiments on established datasets, and can be enhanced further through the presentation of additional state-of-the-art approaches on these platforms. Additionally, a segmentation framework is introduced that integrates various instance segmentation techniques. The paper's key contributions are a comprehensive camouflaged object dataset, an efficient segmentation method, and a benchmark toolkit, as well as the results of comparative experiments to inform future research in the area of camouflaged object segmentation.

In the context of superconductivity, this study focuses on the effects of Lorentz violation. Employing the two-fluid model, we incorporate general Lorentz transformation modifications into the Maxwell equations and BCS theory to establish a Lorentz-infringement parameter, $\xi$. Our research indicates that superconductivity's stability and its breakdown point in the presence of impurities are influenced by $\xi$. Furthermore, for superconductors, the ratio of supercurrent to charge flow is found to depend on $\xi$, offering an experimental opportunity to probe Lorentz-defying phenomena.

As AI's presence in critical systems grows, understanding its limitations is essential for developing robust and reliable technologies, ultimately saving lives.  While AI's benefits are being realized, numerous cases of its failures have been reported, primarily due to a lack of transparency into its performance.  Our solution involves creating an accessible platform for gathering information on AI's errors and developing methods to verify the accuracy of user-submitted error reports.  Our system allows users to submit AI system failure reports and includes several verification mechanisms to gauge the reliability of user-submitted error reports.  Our method enables multiple verification approaches, including user feedback, automated systems, and human evaluation.  Our solution's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study of an interactive storytelling AI system, highlighting the potential of our approach in uncovering AI's mistakes and developing methods to mitigate their errors.

Deep learning object recognition systems often rely on training data that is not sufficient for robust performance in real-world scenarios. This is particularly evident in unfamiliar environments, where systems may misidentify an unfamiliar street sign in a new city. To address this issue, we propose a novel training method that enables a network to learn not only what but also how to recognize a particular object. This approach is based on a stochastic classification routing technique, where each object is associated with a unique routing key. During training, the system learns to recognize these keys and use them to select relevant feature maps. At inference time, the system generates a distribution over possible keys and uses the most probable key to determine how to recognize the object. To ensure efficient computation, we introduce a novel attention module that aggregates key-specific feature maps. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, as the network is able to recognize unseen objects and generalize to new scenarios.

Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of FGSM adversarial training in improving white-box robustness, however, this method still suffers from significant overfitting issues. To address this challenge, a novel approach called ZeroGrad is proposed. This method modifies the FGSM adversarial training process by randomly setting the gradients of a portion of model parameters equal to zero during training, thereby preventing excessive model overfitting. Through analysis, it is revealed that setting the gradients of certain parameters to zero has a profound impact on the model's representation, leading it to focus on the most salient features. This enables the model to distinguish between adversarial examples and normal ones, and to generalize better in the process. Experiments conducted on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets confirm that ZeroGrad significantly reduces overfitting and outperforms state-of-the-art FGSM adversarial training methods.

Our research reveals that a black hole in equilibrium with a surrounding plasma is unlikely to be described by the Thakurta metric, which has been used to re-evaluate the bounds set by LIGO-Virgo on Primordial Black Hole (PBH) merger events. The Thakurta metric deviates from the standard Schwarzschild metric in the vicinity of the event horizon, leading us to question whether these deviations are physically valid. By applying the laws of black hole mechanics, we demonstrate that Thakurta's solution is not consistent with its own initial assumptions. The implications of this finding are significant, as they undermine the argument that PBHs must possess a non-gravitational entropy component, which in turn has been used to set more stringent limits on PBH formation in the early universe.

A persistent change in a problem occurs when the same local minima are consistently found despite changes in the optimization variables, indicating that the problem is stuck in a suboptimal state. This type of change has been identified in previous research as an issue specific to continuous problems. This study expands on this concept by introducing a more relaxed definition of persistent change applicable to discrete problems, which reveals that the black-box search algorithm, CMA-ES, exhibits this issue on a specific problem. The investigation also explores the impact of this type of change on a range of hybrid optimization techniques combining simulated annealing with local search and tabu search with hill climbing, demonstrating that these hybrid methods are not inherently resistant to the persistent change issue.

A key objective of homomorphic encryption is to enable data processing while the data remains encrypted, with various schemes developed to achieve this goal. Despite this goal being in place since the 90s, implementing it without a significant computational cost remains elusive due to the bootstrapping problem, which has only been solved for a specific, limited case. Our work introduces BTS, a fully homomorphic encryption system that streamlines processing through bootstrapping, while significantly reducing complexity. The system relies on a bootstrappable encryption scheme, which also enables a more efficient key generation process. An additional contribution of our work is the development of a fully homomorphic encryption evaluation machine, which can efficiently execute computations on encrypted data.

A specific set of random matrices, denoted as $U_n(a)$, belong to an $n\times n$ complex space and are composed of $2n$ independent random variables on the unit circle. These variables $U_j$ can be seen as a result of rotating a unit-length random vector in a two-dimensional space. The defining characteristic of $U_n(a)$ lies in its associated logarithmic potential, which influences the distribution of the variables: the real part of their product $U_{n-1} U_{n}^{n-1}$ is independent of the sum of their imaginary parts, and follows a Gaussian distribution. The distribution of $U_n(a)$ shares common features with a well-known random matrix ensemble, denoted as the Bessel trio, which itself is an extension of the GUE and CUE matrix ensembles.

The concept of quantum correlation is pivotal in quantum technology and quantum computing. Assessing quantum connections between multiple qubits in realistic devices poses a significant experimental challenge. We investigate the quantum connections between three distinct two-qubit systems, comprised of spin-1 atoms, trapped in optical cavities. By employing homodyne measurement techniques, we analyzed the joint probability distribution of three two-qubit systems, thereby determining the linear quantum correlation metric. As a result, we observed the transition from non-linear to linear quantum correlations at a certain interaction time, a direct consequence of the influence of photon number states. Furthermore, we successfully reconstructed the W state, utilizing a combination of optimal state reconstruction methods, to experimentally confirm the presence of entanglement.

We introduce a novel nonlocality phenomenon known as "decomposability" that diverges from Bell's theorem. Our research reveals three distinct types of decomposable correlations, which can arise from local hidden variables. These types are characterized by the fact that the correlations' local components are not only space-time separated and uncorrelated but are also incapable of generating Bell's inequality. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that these Bell-inequality-violating states can be decomposed as a sum of two states, each of which is also non-Bell states. The key difference between our findings and Bell's theorem lies in the decomposition of these states, which uses different inequalities. Our research also explores the relationship between our proposed phenomenon and monogamy of entanglement and provides a method to experimentally produce these phenomena.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a computationally efficient deep learning pipeline for generating high-definition video. Utilizing a single GPU, StyleGAN-V surpasses existing video synthesis approaches by achieving a 10 times reduction in computational requirements. Our key innovation is a generative model that effectively synthesizes 768x768 images for every frame, comparable to the image-fidelity of StyleGAN2. To facilitate seamless video production, StyleGAN-V features a continuous training process that allows for real-time video generation without the need for re-training. This innovative architecture is paired with a new video sampling algorithm, which leverages the natural video process to direct the sampling process. Our evaluations demonstrate that StyleGAN-V generates video with improved image clarity and realism, while maintaining the characteristic niche specializations of prior video synthesis techniques.

Gurevich and Howe previously introduced the eta Regulator as a pairing element 
in the cohomology of the Heisenberg group, and it provided a connection between 
the cohomology of the Heisenberg group and the cohomology of elliptic curves. 
We are focusing on a restricted version of this pairing, known as the "eta" 
correspondence, which selects a specific element from the cohomology of the 
Heisenberg group. This correspondence has the ability to map the cohomology of 
an elliptic curve to a vector space, and we have established that it preserves 
the degree of elliptic curves, except in one instance where degree 0 is mapped to 
degree -1.

Dosimetry techniques involving luminescence detectors are widely used in various fields such as medical measurement, archaeological research, and scientific research. Researchers have employed deep neural networks to analyze luminescence signals and determine exposure dates more accurately than traditional methods can. By leveraging neural networks to extract relevant data from luminescence signals, scientists can perform complex calculations to estimate exposure dates, thereby simplifying the process of measuring thermal history. This technique has several benefits, including improved accuracy, reduced data requirements, and increased reliability across different locations, materials, and time. The neural network model's effectiveness in various fields has been evaluated using a large dataset comprising 35,000+ glow curves measured at 26+ different locations, and it has been found to achieve high accuracy and precision in exposure date estimations. Furthermore, the model exhibits robust performance across different locations, materials, and time, and its ability to provide accurate results with minimal data is a significant advantage. The model's code and data are available for public access.

We explore the solvability of a nonlinear elliptic problem with singularities arising from non-monotone, double-phase coefficients within the context of Sobolev-Orlicz spaces in a complete manifold. Employing the direct variational method, we establish the existence of weak solutions, accompanied by a proof of their uniqueness and optimal existence bounds via p-semilinear equations within the same Sobolev-Orlicz spaces. Our approach relies on two crucial conditions: the growth of the coefficients being controlled in the double phase by the functionals $\alpha_p$ and $\beta_p$, and the growth of the potential energy being constrained by the functionals $\hat{\alpha}_p$ and $\hat{\beta}_p.

X-ray cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) devices are prevalent in the field of radiation oncology, often used for daily positioning verification. However, they can also be utilized as full-body 3D imaging tools, although their application in this capacity is currently limited due to their typically lower kilovoltage levels compared to the more commonly used medical linear accelerators. The Fastcat CBCT devices, featuring 80 kV and 120 kV X-ray energies, are relatively compact and widely employed for quality assurance and daily positioning purposes. In this study, a simulation tool was developed to model the 3D X-ray absorption patterns of the Fastcat CBCT devices, enabling the generation of digital phantom images representative of the device's absorption characteristics. The simulated images were then compared to the actual X-ray absorption patterns obtained from the Fastcat CBCT devices, revealing a high degree of consistency. The agreement between the simulated and actual image measurements was also found to be statistically significant. The developed simulation tool is anticipated to be a valuable resource for researchers and clinicians looking to leverage the capabilities of the Fastcat CBCT devices for full-body 3D imaging.

Machine learning model explanations have gained significant attention, with numerous methods emerging to interpret them. One widely used approach is LIME, which explains a single prediction by manipulating the data around it. However, this method often introduces out-of-distribution errors, causing users to doubt its accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce S-LIME, a new LIME method that balances clarity with robustness. Unlike other explanations, S-LIME trains a local, interpretable model that is more reliable than its classification function, yet provides clearer insights than a simple linear fit. We demonstrate the effectiveness of S-LIME, showing it surpasses LIME on a range of metrics, including accuracy, interpretability, and robustness. Furthermore, S-LIME improves results for users, increasing their confidence in the predictions and providing a better understanding of the underlying ML system.

In real-world applications, categorization is a fundamental skill that is heavily relied upon for more advanced learning methods. Existing research has shown that people are capable of accurately categorizing concepts and often possess more complex knowledge such as the underlying structures of categorizations. Leveraging this knowledge, we have developed a novel Bayesian model that utilizes justification feedback to not only improve categorization accuracy, but also tap into the existing knowledge of users for more accurate classifications. According to the theory of cumulative learning, users tend to retain information from past experiences, and our model aims to replicate this phenomenon by developing a novel Bayesian approach. By doing so, we have created a system that can effectively utilize justification feedback to not only enhance categorization performance, but also uncover underlying structures in the user's knowledge base.

TbInO$_3$ is a rare-earth spiral metal that, in its paramagnetic state, exhibits a spin-liquid-like structure with triangular-lattice structure and a range of spin-related properties. A recent study using Raman spectroscopy has provided new insights into the spin dynamics of TbInO$_3$, specifically in its paramagnetic state. Observations of two-sphere light scattering patterns suggest the presence of a two-magnon crystal-field excitation, and detailed analysis of the Raman spectrum reveals a collection of vibronic modes linked to a torsional vibration mode. These observations are significant for understanding the spin dynamics of TbInO$_3$, and suggest that its spin-liquid-like properties are closely tied to its electronic and phonetic characteristics.

We investigate a family of modified curvature flows, where a given domain's boundary evolves to minimize its weighted combination of mean curvatures. The weights are chosen from two pre-defined sets: one that ensures the evolving boundary remains convex and another that allows for any weighted flow, excluding self-collapsing or self-terminating ones. For convex flows, we establish a solution existence and a convergence rate to a classical steady state. In contrast, we demonstrate that if the terminal evolution is self-collapsing or self-terminating, then the flow may not converge to a steady state.

A growing number of studies have confirmed that using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze spectral images yields highly effective results. Nonetheless, training such networks remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process. This study proposes an innovative approach to significantly reduce computational requirements when training CNNs in spectral imaging applications. By converting spectral images into a domain where operations are localized in the frequency domain, the need to repeatedly perform high-computational convolution operations is eliminated, allowing for a substantial reduction in computational complexity. Leveraging this approach, we can train CNNs utilizing a more efficient framework that draws inspiration from the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) designed for speech processing in the frequency domain, including the well-known VGGish model. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach, which incorporates the new framework into the VGGish model, can achieve performance comparable to traditional CNNs in spectral imaging applications while reducing computational complexity by a significant margin.

Image clustering and grouping are crucial tasks in computer vision that have seen significant advancements with the emergence of deep neural networks (DNNs). Although previous studies have applied DNNs to image clustering and grouping, they have primarily focused on clustering images from a single group. This paper presents a novel approach, called DeepCluE, that employs a multi-layer DNN framework to tackle image grouping across various groups. The proposed method features a feature extraction layer, a clustering layer, a grouping layer, and a clustering refinement layer, which work together to enhance clustering and grouping performance. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepCluE in image clustering and grouping, particularly in scenarios where the number of groups is known. Additionally, our method exhibits competitive performance compared to other DNN-based approaches in image clustering and grouping.

The potential for risk within an organization is a widespread issue that can manifest in various ways, including through internal and external threats. This research focuses on addressing two key challenges associated with detecting organizational risk: 1) defining a comprehensive risk profile and 2) continuously monitoring for potential risks. We develop a knowledge-based framework that integrates a conceptual model of organizational risk and its root causes with social network analysis and external media coverage. By integrating these components, we create a dynamic risk detection system that can be applied to organizations operating across multiple locations. This system is illustrated through a case study of an international retail company.

Data categorization, a widely employed technique in machine learning, is also a fundamental component of many other data science tasks. The existing categorization methods, however, primarily focus on numerical data and often rely on a two-step process involving clustering followed by classification. This paper presents an innovative clustering technique that simultaneously performs data categorization and clustering using topological data analysis. The approach utilizes the persistent homology of data, representing different levels of data abstraction, to determine a threshold for clustering. By selecting a non-trivial cycle from the persistent homology diagram, any data points that cannot be grouped at this level are placed in separate clusters, while the remaining groups are merged. This method has been successfully applied to high-dimensional medical image data, achieving high accuracy in clustering and classification tasks. The proposed algorithm has been successfully tested on real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness in a variety of applications.

We introduce a language that captures contrasimilarity domains, a broader interpretation of bisimulation domains, and validate its definition by demonstrating its equivalence with domains of alternating games, thereby providing a less complex alternative to Milner's simulation principle. The development of the game language is supported by a type system, which is further established as a denotational semantics by showing that it accurately captures game equivalence.
We utilize the string 2-group framework to illustrate how string and loop identities arise from the string 2-group's properties.

Using the reconnection mechanism, we've created a double pair plasma comprising non-extensive electrons and positive ions. We've then modeled ion-acoustic rogue waves in this system using the non-linear Schrödinger equation to determine their properties. Our research has produced the first-ever analytical rogue wave solutions for this type of double pair plasma. We've also created a stability analysis, incorporating the effects of finite temperature electrons and non-extensive behavior, to determine the plasma's physical parameters. Our investigation has shown that as the non-extensive parameter approaches 1, the rogue wave solutions converge with those in a single pair plasma. We've also confirmed that the rogue waves are physically stable.

A novel approach to model the Alfvén wave parametric decay instability in a plasma is proposed, incorporating both kinetic theory and fluid modeling. By implementing this hybrid model, we can track the evolution of unstable Alfvén waves and their subsequent decay into Alfvénic metaparticles. These meta particles are composed of Alfvén waves and kinetic particles, whose dynamics unfolds in phase space. Upon decay, these meta particles can either persist or lose their coherence and transform back into waves and particles. Our model provides a framework for analyzing the evolution of Alfvén waves and their meta particles, shedding light on their behavior and fate. Applying this model to a specific plasma Q-machine discharge, we demonstrate how the instability arises from significant Alfvén resonance. Furthermore, we observe that the instability is influenced by the presence of kinetic particles, resulting in a nonlinear amplification of meta particles that can persist even after their wave components have decayed.

We investigate the gravitational instability in molecular thread-like nebulae to understand the development of dense and compact regions that can eventually form stars. The initial phase of the nebula is modeled as a non-self-gravitating, linear thread-like perturbation within a background of the equilibrium radial isothermal molecular nebula. The growth rate of the most unstable mode is determined by perturbation theory, taking into account ambipolar diffusion. The results show that the inclusion of ambipolar diffusion significantly reduces the growth rate of the most unstable mode, particularly for thread-like nebulae with low mass-to-flux ratio. The mass-to-flux ratio has a substantial effect on the growth rate, with low ratio leading to increased instability. The inclusion of ambipolar diffusion leads to a lower growth rate compared to scenarios without it, particularly for thread-like nebulae with low mass-to-flux ratio. The gravitational instability in these nebulae is a slow process, with a growth rate that is typically much lower than the rotational frequency. The initial mass-to-flux ratio of the nebula has a substantial effect on the growth rate, with low ratio leading to increased instability. The inclusion of ambipolar diffusion in these nebulae may explain the relatively low density of their compact regions, as it slows down the growth of their density fluctuations.

The quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects are crucial in open quantum dynamics and have significant implications for quantum technologies. Although they have been extensively explored in the case of weak or moderate coupling, a substantial gap exists in our understanding when the strong coupling occurs. This study examines the ZME and AZE phenomena in strong coupling scenarios, with a specific focus on the dynamics of the anharmonic oscillator interacting with light. The investigation reveals that, under specific conditions, the ZME can be activated even in the Markovian regime, and interestingly, this effect can also emerge in the AZe regime under different conditions. The findings also suggest that an increase in system-environment coupling strength may lead to the AZE regime becoming wider, under certain circumstances. These results have important implications for quantum technologies, including quantum information protection and quantum state preparation.

The Heisenberg model, incorporating Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions (DM Heisenberg model), is examined in the context of varying temperatures and an inhomogeneous magnetic field. The research focuses on the spontaneous magnetization, heat capacity, susceptibility, and derived quantities like the Néel temperature, critical exponent, and logarithmic singularity. The findings reveal that a combination of a uniform and variable external field can lead to logarithmically bounded heat capacity and a critical exponent of 1, which is consistent with mean-field behavior. However, when only a uniform field is present, the system behaves like an asymmetric Heisenberg model, exhibiting first-order transitions accompanied by a second-order transition.

Our research presents an internet-based system for planning multi-drone paths, enabling them to navigate around obstacles at an outdoor facility while adhering to specific arrival constraints. The system's core is a distributed planning algorithm that divides the quadrotor swarm into smaller groups and guides each group to avoid obstacles and meet a common objective. To achieve this, we utilize a local planning tool that ensures quadrotors adhere to safety requirements. The overall planning process is facilitated by the Internet and relies on the integration of multiple computational tools, including Viability Analysis, Linear Programming, and the Viability Graph algorithm. The algorithm was tested using a simulated drone swarm and a real-world drone system, both scenarios featuring a group of four quadrotors. The results demonstrated the algorithm's effectiveness in navigating the quadrotors around obstacles and enabling them to meet their target objectives.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is a critical area in machine learning that bridges the gap between the features from source and target domains. This enables the transfer of knowledge from a simulated environment to various real-world settings, where target domain annotations are unavailable. In this study, we introduce CARLANE, a benchmark for evaluating UDA methods in natural navigation tasks, focusing on path detection through visual analysis. We develop a simulation environment that generates diverse path maps and real-world environments with varying visual characteristics, providing extensive variation in domain mapping scenarios. We showcase the effectiveness of a UDA baseline model, pathNet, in adapting simulation features to multiple target domains and outperforming non-adaptive baselines. This demonstrates the potential of our proposed approach.

Our research focuses on how small particles affect the wettability of hydrogels. We examine the angle at which a liquid touches a particle-covered hydrogel and compare it to a pure hydrogel. We develop a mathematical model that explains our findings, and our results indicate that adding particles to a hydrogel makes its surface less slippery. Additionally, we discovered that adding particles to a hydrogel has a unique effect on its surface - it becomes more sensitive to larger liquid drops. These findings suggest that hydrogels could be modified to have specific contact angles by incorporating particles, leading to new applications in controlled drug release.

The abrupt shift to online learning brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted higher education, forcing students to adapt to virtual environments and thereby altering the way they participate in learning activities. This study builds on existing research, which had established a correlation between student engagement and academic performance during pre-pandemic and initial pandemic periods. We extend this relationship to the long-term pandemic era, examining its dynamics in undergraduate psychology courses. By comparing data from three consecutive academic periods - two prior to the pandemic and one after - we observed a persistent correlation between student engagement and academic performance. Interestingly, student engagement correlated strongly with academic performance during the initial pandemic but the correlation weakened significantly with the introduction of in-person learning, suggesting students were more motivated to learn when classes were online. This study reinforces previous findings, providing new insights into the relationship between student engagement and academic performance in a pandemic context, and offering practical advice for educators on harnessing this connection to enhance learning outcomes.

The wind speed profile in the upper atmosphere of stars like V374 Peg is a crucial parameter for modeling the accretion process in young stars.  The conventional method of measuring this profile involves ground-based optical line-blaze Doppler spectroscopy, which is prone to errors due to its limitations in signal-to-noise ratio and the presence of atmospheric interference.  In contrast, our study presents a new approach to measuring the wind speed using radio continuum flux density data at L-band.  The data from V374 Peg shows that the wind speed in the outer atmosphere is consistent with the inner atmosphere values obtained through optical spectroscopy, and the analysis also reveals a strong correlation between the optical and radio wind speed profiles.  By combining the optical and radio data, the model can be more accurately fitted, and the inclusion of the L-band data enables the detection of the convection zone inversion.  The study demonstrates that the L-band data can be a valuable supplementary tool for measuring the wind speed in the outer atmosphere of young stars.

We have analyzed spectroscopic data of 85 stars in the UBC 274 cluster, obtained from the Gaia-ESO Survey, covering the mass range from 0.13 to 0.70 solar masses. Employing the binary-star decontamination method, we identified 42 likely cluster members, which we used to investigate the kinematic and chemical state of the UBC 274 cluster, which is characterized by an age of 0.63 Gyr and a metallicity of -0.92. The cluster's rotational velocity is approximately 0.64 km/s, and it is situated about 0.8 kpc from the Sun. Notably, the UBC 274 cluster is about to dissolve within the next 0.23 Gyr. Furthermore, the abundance of alpha, iron-peak, and beta elements in the UBC 274 cluster is significantly lower than that in the solar neighborhood and the solar SMC. The oxygen abundance in the UBC 274 cluster is consistent with that in the solar SMC, while the abundance of the alpha elements is significantly lower than that in the solar SMC. The oxygen abundance in the UBC 274 cluster is also correlated with the stellar mass, which is consistent with the idea that the UBC 274 cluster is undergoing dissolution.

Evaluating the effectiveness of machine translation (MT) models in enhancing text corpus quality is a complex task. In this research, we investigate how well MT models perform in assessing the quality of a large English-German corpus. We examine whether our findings have any general applicability to other languages and languages pairings. To do this, we utilize multiple quality metrics to analyze the improved corpus. We also determine whether the benefits of improved corpus quality in neural machine translation (NMT) are evident. Our results reveal that the MT models' ability to evaluate corpus quality is dependent on several factors including the language pair and whether the MT model is trained on the specific corpus in question.

We explore a novel phenomenon where an external driving force induces a rapid
transition from an entangled state to a less entangled state. This scenario is
realized by modifying the Hamiltonian of a one-dimensional spin chain with
nearest-neighbour interactions using a time-dependent control method. We propose
a general approach to drive such a system towards a less entangled state in the
long-term limit. We demonstrate that the effect of this driving can be tailored to
result in a wide variety of long-term entanglement shifts, including completely
erasing entanglement. We study the time it takes for the system to reach this
limit and how it depends on the system's parameters. We also identify a critical
point that marks the transition from a substantial shift in entanglement to no
shift at all. We apply our approach to the transverse Ising model, which is a
well-known model for magnetism and quantum phase transitions. We find that the
long-term entanglement shift is influenced by the correlation length of the
underlying magnetism and exhibits a complex dependence on the system's parameters.
Moreover, we find that the shift can be either logarithmically or linearly
dependent on the control strength, depending on the system's parameters.

The interaction between electrons and their spin-orbit velocity, a fundamental phenomenon found in various solids, has significant implications for electronic, magnetic, and optoelectronic properties. In two-dimensional materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides, this interaction leads to distinct effects, notably the presence of ferromagnetic order in bilayers and the formation of valley-polarized states in bulk crystals. A recent study has investigated the spin-orbit interaction in flat bands of transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures, revealing that it gives rise to a variety of novel phenomena. These include the emergence of unconventional superconductivity, topological phases, and magnetic effects, which are influenced by the flat-band nature of the electrons. This work provides an overview of the spin-orbit interaction in these heterostructures, focusing on theoretical approaches that are applicable to flat bands.

A novel algorithm, known as the Quantum Reservoir Processing (QRP) algorithm, is developed to optimize quantum systems. This algorithm functions as a control mechanism for master equations describing open quantum systems, particularly those influenced by self-adjoint friction. QRP can be utilized to minimize the steady-state kinetic energy of a system interacting with a high-temperature reservoir. This is achieved by pre-calculating control pulses that optimize control for system states with low kinetic energy. Results demonstrate that QRP-based control outperforms traditional optimal control methods, particularly when considering high energies. This difference in performance is attributed to the algorithm's ability to convey system dynamics information to the high-energy subspace through the reservoir, thus enabling lower control energies. Additionally, QRP-based control allows for the manipulation of system dynamics in the subspace, which is not possible with standard optimal control methods. This research highlights the benefits of the QRP algorithm and its potential applications in simulating complex quantum systems.

Gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductors have garnered significant interest for their use in electronic devices, particularly due to their exceptional high-power, high-temperature, and radiation-resistance capabilities. On-silicon-sapphire substrates, which offer cost savings and improved performance by eliminating lattice-mismatch-related defects, are being considered as viable alternatives to traditional substrates. Nonetheless, achieving atom confinement within the GaN crystal is crucial for studying a variety of properties, such as quantum effects. Our study proposes a method for atom confinement within the GaN crystal by employing a focused ion beam, which we validated through experiments. Results indicate that, utilizing a 30 keV beam, Ga ions can be used to create confined structures in the GaN crystal, which we measured by analyzing the energy distribution of secondary electrons. Our findings reveal that the spatial resolution of the etched structures in the GaN crystal is approximately 10 nm, which we were able to achieve by adjusting the scanning parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrated the ability to create complex confined structures in the GaN crystal through layer-by-layer etching, which we achieved by adjusting the scanning parameters and utilizing a lift-off technique. Our proposed method has the potential to enable a variety of applications, such as nanotechnology and device fabrication.

Two distinct finite element methods are explored in this investigation: Lagrange and Mixed Finite Elements. Lagrange Finite Elements solve for both velocity and pressure variables within a single set of equations, whereas Mixed Finite Elements break down the pressure into an auxiliary set of variables, thereby improving the stability of velocity field discretization. However, the choice of curvilinear mesh geometry plays a significant role in determining the optimal choice of these elements. This study compares the performance of these elements on a range of problems, from simple Stokes flow to complex fluid dynamics involving solid objects and time-dependent flows past cylinders.

We investigate the dynamics of a particular class of sign-alterable dark energy models, which exhibit altered behavior in dark energy interactions. These models are characterized by a novel interaction term, which can vary in sign and is dependent on the evolution of a certain scalar field. The presence of the sign-alterable interaction term allows the model to capture the late-time acceleration of the universe without being restricted to a specific sign. Our analysis reveals that the model can successfully explain the late-time acceleration of the universe, while its early-time behavior depends on the chosen initial conditions. Furthermore, the model can be distinguished from other theories of dark energy based on the dynamics of certain key indices.

The observed radio bursts from TDEs are short-lived, intense, could be randomly occurring, and could be detected over a broad frequency range. We investigate the possibility that these bursts are triggered by the outburst of a TDE passing through the interstellar medium. The radio bursts from a shock-driven jet can be generated by synchrotron radiation from accelerated particles. The radio bursts from a TDE can be explained by the synchrotron radiation from particles accelerated by the interstellar medium's shock wave impinging on the expanding jet. The radio bursts from a TDE can be explained by the synchrotron radiation from particles accelerated by the interstellar medium's shock wave impinging on the expanding jet. The duration of the radio bursts from a TDE can be explained by the synchrotron radiation from a shock-driven jet with a magnetic field of 10 micro Gauss and a Lorentz factor of 50. The energy of the radio bursts from a TDE can be explained by the synchrotron radiation from a shock-driven jet with a Lorentz factor of 50 and a magnetic field of 10 micro Gauss.

Acoustic cavitation involves the formation and subsequent collapse of micro-bubbles in a liquid when subjected to high-amplitude, intermittent sound waves. The energy released by their collapse can generate temperatures high enough to initiate chemical reactions, which has significant potential across various fields. The rapid collapse of the bubble creates a transient pressure increase that is extremely challenging to model mathematically. In this study, we investigate the transient behavior of acoustic cavitation in a finite liquid domain, where a single bubble is introduced at the center of a spherical tank. We use a computational approach based on the Navier-Stokes equations to examine the dynamics of the fluid and bubble system, and we use this approach to analyze the pressure distribution and bubble dynamics during the acoustic cavitation process.

In our research, we introduce MUSER, a novel dataset centered on tension recognition and recognition in high-stakes interactive scenarios. MUSER uniquely incorporates real-time multimodal input, including non-verbal cues like facial expressions, hand gestures, and physiological signals. Our dataset features a comprehensive range of tension levels, encompassing both common and extreme scenarios, with 45 participants across 18 tasks, resulting in 1,260 minutes of data. To enhance the dataset, we introduce an emotion acknowledgment task, requiring models to not only identify user tension but also to infer intended messages. We also propose a baseline model demonstrating the value of incorporating the emotion acknowledgment task, showcasing its potential to boost performance. MUSER is now available for public access at https://www.facebook.com/open-source/muser.

Developing artificial intelligence for graph structures within complex systems is a critical challenge for scientists and engineers.  The field has largely focused on static graph analysis, but dynamic graph learning is now gaining traction.  Nonetheless, creating realistic and effective graph datasets within controlled environments remains a significant hurdle.  To address this, we have developed PanGEA, a comprehensive, expandable, and scalable toolset for designing, executing, and annotating dynamic graph experiments.  This graph-based simulation environment leverages a container-based approach to model complex systems and their associated graph structures.  PanGEA's graphical interface streamlines the process of setting up simulations, while its dynamic graph manager efficiently models temporal relationships between nodes.  PanGEA's annotation toolkit utilizes the Open Graph Benchmark to evaluate and validate the generated datasets.  This paper delves into the core components of PanGEA, highlighting its potential for the scientific computing community through real-world examples.

We used a model that simulates the evolution of galaxies by merging smaller units into larger ones, with each unit's star formation rate determined by its mass, metal content, and environmental conditions.
