This collection, dubbed Robin after the title character from Steel Magnolias, contains 476,894 annotated suicidal texts extracted from Twitter, along with 1.64 million non-suicidal comparison texts. Each text is accompanied by a risk assessment score based on the language and sentiment used. This publicly available dataset has the potential to enhance the development of machine learning-based mental health monitoring tools.

A novel framework is proposed that reconciles the principles of quantum mechanics with the standard Black Hole model. In this framework, a central entity governs the behavior of Hawking temperatures across all black holes. This approach yields a range of testable outcomes, including specific temperatures for each existing black hole type. A secondary aspect of this framework is a new theoretical framework, termed Blackian mechanics, whose underlying principles are entirely unknown. This framework successfully explains the entropy of a particular type of black hole, a phenomenon not yet explained by any existing theories.

This paper's objective is to produce bounded solutions for a specific difference equation, $x_{n+1}=a x^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1},0<\alpha \leq2$. The equation $x_{n+1}=a x^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$ has been applied in medicine to model cell growth dynamics by considering $a=x_0, b=x_1$ and $\alpha=2$. The equation's solutions in the case of medicine have been analyzed in a bounded setting. The current paper's focus is on determining bounded solutions for the equation $x_{n+1}=a x^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$ for $\alpha=2$ and any $a \in \mathbb R, b \in \mathbb R, \alpha \in (0,2)$.

We develop a consistent, spherically symmetric solution framework for a Born-Infeld-type electrodynamic theory in an anti-de Sitter spacetime, encompassing a wide range of nonlinear electrodynamic theories. This solution is characterized by a range of parameters, including the Born-Infeld parameter, and two additional dimensionless parameters. We demonstrate the existence of charged black holes within this framework, classifying them based on different values of the Born-Infeld parameter. We then investigate the thermodynamic properties of these black holes, including their entropies and temperatures. We also examine the effect of the Born-Infeld parameter on the thermodynamic behavior of these black holes. We find that the thermodynamic behavior of these black holes exhibits universal features, independent of the Born-Infeld parameter. We also find that the thermodynamic properties of these black holes are in agreement with the principles of the holographic c-theorem.

A specific type of arrangement $\mathcal{A}$, known as the Sidon arrangement, is defined within a vector space when certain specific hyperplanes are included. The resulting arrangement's characteristic polynomial is also given. The Sidon arrangement's structure is studied in depth, including a general method for describing the intersection of various hyperplanes. The outcome of this intersection gives rise to a new polyhedron, known as a "cut-polytope." A formula is derived to estimate the number of facets present in this cut-polytope. The result is further refined for scenarios where the vector space is of a specific dimension. The resulting conditions are described using a measure-theoretic concept. The resulting conditions are also shown to be equivalent to a scenario where a particular type of set is structured in a specific geometric manner. The resulting conditions are also shown to be equivalent to a scenario where a particular type of set is structured in a specific geometric manner.

The magnetic susceptibility of the two-dimensional XY model is calculated using a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and the functional-integral approach introduced by Kogut and Wilson. At finite temperatures, our analysis of the susceptibility yields results in agreement with existing findings, particularly regarding its behavior at lower temperatures. Furthermore, within the framework of the functional-intial approach, some insights are gained into the temperature dependence of the Chern number in a disk-shaped system, although a conclusive understanding remains elusive.

Our study focused on the Ising model's behavior on simple cubic lattices, where we examined the reversal process from a paramagnetic state to a ferromagnetic state. We discovered an unexpected relationship between the initial temperature and relaxation time, showing that a slight increase in temperature can lead to a longer relaxation time. This phenomenon was observed in simulations using the Metropolis and Wolff algorithms, and it contradicts what might be intuitively expected. To explain this effect, we considered the impact of larger clusters or "domain walls" on the relaxation process, where an increase in temperature could reduce domain wall movement, resulting in a longer relaxation time.

We investigate the motion of a coupled particle in a one-dimensional disordered potential, specifically a quasicrystalline disorder sequence. The disorder arises from a random sequence of energy levels generated by a non-linear map, with a characteristic period determined by an integer $q$ that leads to a quasi-periodic sequence. The motion of the coupled particle is modeled by a non-Markovian hopping process, with a power-law dependence on the energy gap between sites. Using a mathematical approach, we derive the localization exponent $\zeta$ for this system by analyzing the eigenfunctions of the corresponding Schrödinger operator. The results show that, for large $q$, the localization exponent behaves as $\zeta(q) \sim q^{-\theta}$, where $\theta$ is a constant. This exponent determines the rate at which localization increases with increasing quasi-periodic order $q$. The obtained results are consistent with numerical simulations.

Conversational AI systems using natural language are becoming increasingly popular, especially chatbots that cater to specific objectives. These systems, also known as task-focused conversation systems, are expected to not only comprehend and generate natural language inputs but also provide users with precise and informative responses. A notable example is a virtual assistant that uses natural language to assist users in planning itineraries, answering queries such as "Book a flight from New York to Los Angeles on the second weekend of August." To efficiently process such language inputs, these systems often rely on pre-trained multilingual language models that can handle various languages. This survey aims to outline the underlying challenges and significant advancements in NLP for task-oriented dialogues, especially in multilingual settings, offering a comprehensive overview of the field for researchers.

To uncover the mechanisms governing alternative splicing, we developed a computational approach that relies on the comparison of individual transcript expression profiles. This approach enables the identification of differential splicing events, which reveal how alternative transcripts differ in their abundance and how these differences are regulated. Through a comprehensive analysis of short-term RNA sequencing data from mice, we found that most alternative transcripts exhibit distinct patterns of expression variation. These patterns were observed not only across different conditions but also within individual time points, indicating a high level of temporal regulation. Furthermore, we found that the expression variation of alternative splicing events is often associated with the regulation of other alternative forms, suggesting that alternative splicing is part of a complex network of regulatory mechanisms.

The issue of data protection has been a persistent concern within the information systems field.  While various data protection frameworks exist, their implementation is often hindered by the lack of clear guidelines for specific industries.  In the financial sector, certain regulatory requirements are outlined in standard documents, but the concrete steps to ensure compliance are not clearly defined.  In order to clarify the financial industry's data protection standards, researchers conducted in-depth interviews with industry professionals.  The study found that financial institutions are aware of key data protection principles but struggle with understanding what actions they need to take to ensure compliance.  In fact, it is often left to individual business units to determine their own data protection policies.  In light of this, researchers proposed a series of concrete steps to help financial institutions achieve data protection, covering the initial stages of data protection preparation and the ongoing monitoring of data protection standards.  The study highlights the importance of data protection in the financial sector and suggests that information systems researchers should engage in data protection research that is tailored to the financial industry's specific needs.

We examine the formation of harmonic coefficients $v_n$ in multiparticle collisions between protons and gold nuclei at high energy. By simulating the very first $pA$ collisions at the Future Circular Collider, we found that the coefficients for $n=2$ and $n=3$ are primarily influenced by the initial proton-nucleus collision and subsequent particle production. The coefficients are largely unaffected by the presence of a magnetic field and depend only on the energy of the incoming proton beam. As a result, we suggest using the coefficients for $n=2$ and $n=3$ as indicators of the initial proton-nucleus collision.

Investigating the creation of light nuclei in collisions between gold atoms, we utilized the VENUS-MP model to examine the process at an energy of 3 GeV. Our findings indicate that the production of deuterons, tritons, and helium-3 is largely influenced by the expansion of the system and the initial conditions of the collision. The abundance of these light nuclei in the final stages of the system depends on the extent of thermal equilibrium and the initial conditions of the collision. Furthermore, we discovered that the production of these light nuclei is significantly affected by the presence of baryon density at the end of the system. The production of these light nuclei is also influenced by the freeze-out of nucleons, resulting in a complex interplay of coalescence origins.

The study of exoplanets has significantly advanced our understanding of planetary science, particularly with regards to the types of planets and systems that exist beyond our solar system.  A key area of focus has been on terrestrial planets similar in size to Earth, with numerous exoplanets having been discovered in recent years.  These findings have provided a wealth of information regarding the diversity of environments that may exist on terrestrial planets, including those that are thought to be similar to Earth.  In this review, we explore the current state of knowledge regarding the atmospheric and oceanic environments that are expected to exist on stony exoplanets, including those that are thought to be similar to Earth.  We examine the constraints that are placed on these environments by observations of the planets' radii, orbits, and other attributes, as well as the implications that have been drawn from them.  We also discuss the potential for future research to further refine our understanding of the diverse environments that may exist on terrestrial planets.

A novel approach has been developed to determine the solvability of circulant graphs by their prime factors. This method involves identifying a solvable finite group that corresponds to the central element of the graph's adjacency matrix. Building on previous research, particularly focusing on 2-cyclic structures, a subset of circulant graphs where two specific prime factors dominate (p^a q^b), a new theorem has been established. It states that a particular type of graph, G, is solvable if and only if its automorphism group's centralizer contains the graph G itself. Consequently, a key application of this theorem reveals that specific prime-power circulant graphs, derived from two prime numbers p and q, are solvable if and only if the automorphism group of G has a centralizer that includes the graph G itself.

This study introduces an enhanced approach to iterative matrix inversion, expanding upon a previous method [1] to facilitate matrix dimensions of several thousand. The proposed framework accommodates large matrix dimensions by capitalizing on rapid computation during flight operations and extensive memory storage capabilities in onboard computers or external systems, such as data logging devices. The framework's execution speed is primarily constrained by the rate of matrix-vector multiplications, which can reach 1 ms for 2000x2000 matrix dimensions. The framework's utility is demonstrated through applications such as correcting image distortion, applying correction filters, and performing signal smoothing, while also allowing for real-time processing of external sensor data. The framework's adaptive nature enables it to be easily transferred to other aircraft systems, such as autopilot systems, to support aircraft command generation.

During inflation, ultra-slow-roll inflation can generate a wide range of primordial disturbances with significant power spectra, leading to severe stochastic instability. This study investigates the energy spectrum of these disturbances under the influence of back reaction, revealing that the energy spectrum of ultra-slow-roll inflation deviates from a Gaussian distribution and that the amplitude of perturbations peaks at a specific frequency. The study provides analytical formulas to describe the energy spectrum and reveals that, in the presence of back reaction, the energy spectrum of ultra-slow-roll inflation deviates from a typical power-law shape, instead peaking at a specific frequency and then decreasing.

We've identified a significant issue in ensemble selection with an emphasis on both the accuracy and performance of the model. This issue is more severe than previously acknowledged, particularly when considering large datasets, which can lead to an explosion of potential candidates, resulting in computationally infeasible solution spaces. Our investigation into various optimization techniques for this problem reveals that some methods show promise, such as evolutionary algorithms and the sequential selection procedure, but require further exploration. Notably, evolutionary algorithms offer a notable improvement over traditional approaches, and our computational study suggests that they may be a suitable alternative. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis of the sequential selection procedure reveals that it can be simplified into a more tractable form, which can be efficiently solved by established methods.

The R package casebase provides a unique statistical analysis method, focusing on evaluating the reliability of disease prediction models at various risk levels, as well as comparing the performance of different models. The package's core feature is the case-based analysis, which calculates and graphs a disease risk score for each individual in the dataset, with the score ranging from 0 to 1. This analysis is based on the logistic model and allows for the incorporation of external covariates. In addition, the package enables the comparison of disease risk probabilities across different time periods and calculation of the number of true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives at a specified risk level. The package's case-based analysis is particularly suited for evaluating survival times and supports time-dependent covariates.

This study evaluates the accuracy requirements for computing Feynman integrals used in theoretical high-energy physics computations. To evaluate the requirements, we consider several key factors including computation complexity and precision needs, computation scale, and the necessity for public results available to the entire physics community. Based on these evaluations, we recommend minimum precision requirements of 4 significant figures in most cases, with higher precision needed in certain scenarios. The results of this study apply to both analytical and numerical computations.

The increasing volume of data from High Energy Physics experiments poses significant storage challenges. With data rates reaching 25 TB/s and a projected 100 TB object store capacity, both Lustre and DAOS are being considered as potential solutions. This study aims to compare the performance of these two systems for storing and preserving HEP object data. To achieve this, a comprehensive test plan has been devised to evaluate the data management capabilities of both object stores under standard and realistic scenarios. To validate the test plan, a simplified data management system is being developed, and data samples from the Large Hadron Collider, comprising 5 TB to 10 TB files, are being used. By applying the test plan, the performance of both object stores can be evaluated, particularly in terms of data access patterns, data sizes, and file operations. The data collection will be completed in two rounds, and the first round's findings will be presented in this study. The data collected in the second round will focus on simulating real-world scenarios, including the impact of network latency and data management on the object stores.

A novel system for electric vehicles has been introduced at a prominent downtown parking garage in Los Angeles, offering reduced fees and enhanced incentives to encourage the widespread adoption of EVs. The system, referred to as EVCS, utilizes a virtual queueing approach to enable electric vehicles to reserve parking spaces and receive discounted rates. By centralizing the system, EVCS enables the integration of various parking lots, allowing users to reserve and monitor their parking spaces in real-time across multiple garages. The EVCS system, designed to increase the accessibility and convenience of public parking for EVs, utilizes a cloud-based platform and mobile app to support its operations.

This paper builds on a 2019 study by Huang et al. demonstrating the possibility of optimizing the minimum distance within a specific class of linear codes based on a given condition. The work extends this concept to a broader class of LCD codes and novel linear codes, with an emphasis on developing interactive coding techniques, and presents an algorithmic method for constructing LCD codes through extension and covering processes.

We propose a statistical model that explains the gravitational behavior of sources with minimal gravity based on the statistical properties of random loops in spacetime, which exhibit topological structure. The model relies on the understanding that random loop interactions in spacetime tend to form continuous surfaces due to their inherent topological structure. The surface tension generated by these loops in spacetime gives rise to the gravitational field, and our calculations show that this model predicts a gravitational potential that is directly proportional to the inverse square of the distance between sources, a classic $1/r^2$ behavior. Additionally, our model provides an explanation for the observed surface tension at the Casimir window, which has been measured to be as low as $10^{-10}$ N/m$^2$ in certain Casimir experiments.

The expansion of renewable energy sources is crucial for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the Western United States, but this growth poses a risk of encroaching on the National Wilderness and Wilderness Study Areas, potentially harming outdoor enthusiasts. To tackle this concern, we created the American West Decarbonization Model, which optimizes the use of 12 different renewable energy sources and considers the impact on 10 national parks and other wilderness areas. To mitigate these spatial trade-offs, we developed a sophisticated method that incorporates the construction of wind farms and solar panels into the model. Our analysis revealed that decarbonizing the power grid by 2050 could result in various scenarios, including the construction of renewable energy sources in some national parks and hotspots in Arizona and Nevada to minimize disruptions to outdoor activities.

Cluster-randomized trials are frequently employed to evaluate the effectiveness of immunization programs, but estimating their treatment effect is complicated by within-cluster correlations. According to the Cochran formula, this leads to an estimator that deviates from the intention-to-treat measure, focusing on average program effects across clusters. However, this estimator may not accurately represent the treatment effects experienced by individual units within the clusters. We introduce a new approach, termed individual-level direct randomization, which enables direct inference about various key treatment outcomes for individuals, including the probability of adverse events and the occurrence of specific diseases, from single-arm cluster-randomized trials. Furthermore, this direct randomization framework can be utilized to estimate cumulative adverse event rates and the incidence of constant end-points over multiple observation periods. We also propose a method to deduce individual-level inferences from the cluster-level estimator, and demonstrate its limitations.

We propose an innovative fractal family, known as the Mobius Octagonal Network, derived from the well-known Octagonal Network, which is a Charlap-Warshel family variant. This proposed network is characterized by exponential growth in its degree and eigenvalue spectra as the generation increases. Furthermore, we establish that the Laplacian spectra of these networks possess two distinct symmetry properties. Building upon these findings, we investigate the Laplacian spectra of Octagonal-type networks, leveraging the symmetry and exponential growth properties of our proposed network. This research yields a set of conjectures regarding the Laplacian spectra of Octagonal-type networks, encompassing standardized Z-eigenvalue spectra, symmetry properties, and exponential symmetry-based symmetry properties. These conjectures are expected to be confirmed through future studies.

We examine a scenario where multiple agents, located in different environments, must solve similar contextual decision-making problems. Each agent receives a reward signal influenced by their environment's unique characteristics, which they must learn and adapt to despite never observing rewards from other environments. We present a distributed online learning algorithm that enables agents to adapt to their environment's specific features without needing to know the settings' dimensions. This algorithm allows agents to achieve sublinear regret without requiring them to know the settings' dimensions. We then apply this algorithm to a variety of agents, each using a different model, and show that a generalization of a widely known online learning algorithm is indeed an instance of a mirror descent method.

Creating digital health records from external studies is crucial for precise clinical decision-making and developing new treatments, but it often remains unclear how the patient population was selected. As a result, externally-sourced electronic health records might not be representative of the population of interest, potentially leading to unreliable conclusions and potentially hazardous treatment decisions. Informed decision-making relies on understanding the characteristics of the patient population. In this study, we aimed to determine if the patient population in a clinical trial with a bronchodilator therapy was similar to a larger population of cystic fibrosis patients. By comparing the two groups, we could select a more relevant control population for future studies. Using data from the CF Foundation's Patient Registry, we identified key differences between the two groups and then utilised the Synthetic Population Generator to generate a synthetic population that closely resembles the control group.

The decay patterns of $D^{0} \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ have been extensively examined by LHCb in a comprehensive study. A novel method of analysis has been developed to identify the primary sources of decay through the production of known $D$-meson resonances. A detailed investigation into the three- and four-particle modes has been conducted, focusing on the characteristics of the $\bar{K}^{*0}(800)^+$ and $K_0^0(800)^{-}$ states, which are predicted by the Chiral Unitary Theory. Furthermore, a comprehensive review of the $D^0$ decay to $K^0_S \pi^+\pi^-$, $K^0_S \pi^+\pi^-\pi^-$, and $K^- \pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ channels reveals the presence of the $K(1460)$ and $D_s^0$ resonances, which are in line with predictions from the Large Hadron Colliderb's current understanding of the $D$-meson decay dynamics.

This research presents Novelpy, a pioneering open-source tool for assessing citation-based originality and disruptiveness in various fields such as publications, drugs, and innovations. By employing novel citation analysis techniques, Novelpy's Python library offers innovative methods for evaluating scientific and technological value. A comprehensive benchmarking study validates the effectiveness of different schemes, demonstrating that citation-based and reference-based models yield consistent results. The findings highlight the superiority of citation-based schemes in measuring originality and disruptiveness, particularly when compared to reference-based approaches. This work provides a foundation for future developments and showcases Novelpy's capabilities, including its ability to analyze complex datasets and offer insights on value creation in fields such as pharmaceuticals.

To fine-tune the output of multiple lasers, we introduce a method where the power levels of a multitude of laser sources are adjusted in unison both in time and in space. To achieve this, a master laser is used to control the behavior of the secondary lasers through the process of cross-phase modulation. By dividing a laser beam into numerous sub-beams and directing them at distinct points, it becomes feasible to create a single laser beam with a variable intensity pattern. The intensity distribution of the generated beam is controlled by the behavior of the secondary laser source, which is influenced by the behavior of the master laser source at different points in time. The technique can be utilized for applications in laser communication where the power level is adjusted according to the data being transmitted.

A computer vision system is developed to predict the trajectory of arrows fired from a recurve bow during Olympic-level competitions, utilizing OpenCV and a trained media pipeline. This system is tested using a kink-tipped arrow and a camera with a resolution of 720p, capturing images at 60 frames per second, while also accounting for environmental factors, including air resistance and initial arrow velocity. Using a trained neural network based on UNet architecture, the system is tested with both synthetic and real-world images, achieving high accuracy on synthetic data but facing challenges with real-world data due to camera limitations and variable angles.

Online platforms utilizing recommender systems face a dual challenge of accurately predicting user preferences while maintaining efficient data processing. To address this issue, in the context of cross-domain recommendation, researchers have employed transfer learning to integrate domain-specific models. A novel approach is proposed to train a single, efficient model that leverages dual representations of user and item data across domains. By employing a dual metric learning technique, the proposed method, called DualMTR, can effectively learn domain-invariant embeddings and enhance recommendation accuracy. Comprehensive experiments on two large datasets demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of DualMTR, with notable improvements in prediction accuracy and significant reductions in computational requirements.

We introduce a novel framework, referred to as ASYNC-DA, which represents a type of decentralized automaton capable of simulating the behavior of distributed systems with asynchronous interactions. The proposed framework is shown to effectively model a wide range of such systems. By drawing parallels with the concept of mu-calculus, we establish that ASYNC-DEA share similar expressiveness, and further establish a tight bound on their ability to express. The proposed ASYNC-DEA framework is demonstrated to effectively model a wide range of decentralized systems with a high degree of expressiveness, and is capable of modeling systems with a high degree of complexity.

This paper explores the concept of heat transfer in the context of steady-state diffusion within a two-dimensional plasma array. The array consists of a regular, hexagonal structure with a repeating pattern of voids and metal columns. The metal columns are linked by a network of resistive nanowires. The study examines the heat flow through these nanowires, assuming they operate under uniform thermal conditions and utilizing a precise mathematical framework. The analysis reveals that heat flow through the nanowires can be modeled by a specific set of equations, taking into account their spatial arrangement and physical properties. The results suggest that heat flow in the plasma array can be optimized by adjusting the size and number of voids, while maintaining a consistent temperature across the entire structure. The findings have the potential to inform the development of novel thermal management systems for nanoscale devices.

We investigate the probability that a linear combination of data vectors, derived from a given set of training points, results in a specific target point. This problem has practical applications in topics such as computational geometry, machine learning, and statistics. By utilizing the concept of a Voronoi diagram, we are able to provide an exact solution for the case of halfspace classification, while for the full classification problem, we offer approximate solutions. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence to support the accuracy of our methods, specifically through experiments involving the MNIST dataset, the UCI dataset, and the Gaia dataset, resulting in consistent outcomes that are both efficient and accurate.

Cardiac angiography via fluoroscopy is widely used for both diagnostic and interventional procedures. Fluoroscopic imaging, though effective, exposes patients and medical professionals to high levels of X-ray radiation, posing significant health risks. In this research, we propose a deep-learning based approach to decrease the X-ray radiation dosage during cardiac angiography via video interpolation. Given that fluoroscopic images exhibit temporal coherence, the method involves generating missing images in a sequence by learning the future image's characteristics from a sequence of images. Our approach is based on a recurrent U-Net architecture, where we incorporate a custom loss function to minimize X-ray radiation dosage. Experiment results demonstrate that our method can generate acceptable images with 10% to 20% lower radiation levels, while also showing a high level of visual similarity to ground truth images.

Heavy-flavor production at a future electron-positron collider like the FCC-ee offers significant opportunities for physics research, including precise measurements of the CKM unitarity triangle and the charm quark form factor. However, these measurements depend heavily on the accuracy of theoretical predictions, which currently fall short of what is required. The need for more advanced hadronic QCD calculations has become evident and several approaches are being explored to enhance existing perturbative methods. The main challenges and potential solutions to these challenges will be presented in this talk, including the application of resummation and reswitching techniques, as well as the integration of new physics processes, such as the "soft-gluon vertex" and "single soft" corrections.

The lepton flavor violating processes $\mu\to e\gamma$ and $\mu-N\to e-N$ are predicted to have rates within experimental detection limits when considering the extended gauge theory $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ and a 220 MeV mass for the associated $Z^\prime$ boson. The required boost in $\mu\to e\gamma$ signal is achieved through a substantial 6-7 order of magnitude enhancement resulting from the nearby mass of the $\tau$ lepton acting as a quantum mechanical tunneling factor. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the $\mu-N\to e-N$ process is heavily suppressed by the massive barrier in the $\tau$ sector, effectively resolving the long-standing problem of the neutrino mass hierarchy.

We investigate the possibility of observed high-velocity stars originating from the Milky Way's core through the effect of long-term gravitational perturbations caused by an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH). Utilizing a set of N-body simulations that incorporate an IMBH with a mass of approximately $8\times 10^5$ solar masses, we examine the evolution of the halo and its potential for hosting stars with extremely high velocities. Our findings suggest that the IMBH's presence results in the ejection of approximately $5\times 10^{-2} M_\odot$ per million years, which is consistent with the observed rate of high-velocity stars within the Galaxy's halo. These ejected stars can have velocities of up to several hundred kilometers per second, and are likely to originate from the halo's inner regions. Moreover, the IMBH's effect leads to the formation of a distinct ring structure within the halo's inner 20 kiloparsecs, which is characterized by a high eccentricity and a significant difference in velocity, resulting in the formation of a bipolar structure. This process is a potential explanation for the observed asymmetry in the Milky Way's core, which is a common feature in various simulations.

This paper examines a specific SDE, specifically a multiplicative stochastic differential equation with singular coefficients, to demonstrate its existence. To handle the singularity, a novel mathematical approach is introduced, and it reveals the utility of a previously proposed method known as regularization by disturbance. This technique, initially developed to solve differential equations, can also effectively address such equations, and its integration with semigroup theory yields positive outcomes for the given scenario.

The definability of the Poincar\'{e} axiom for $\omega_1$ has been established
independently by Galvin and Prikry, and this result stems from their earlier
work. We examine whether similar findings can be applied to the Cofinality
Axiom and the Shelah schema, and discuss how these results relate to the
general principles of abstract Hilbert algebras. We present an alternative
proof of Prikry's theorem that aligns with the axioms of distributive lattice
theory, and this approach has been used to derive a new theorem of Kanamori.
Notably, our findings are limited by the $\Delta_2^1$-analogue of the Cofinality
Axiom, and attempts to expand beyond this boundary have been unsuccessful.
Additionally, we demonstrate that the $\Sigma_2^1$-Shelah schema is not
equivalent to its $\Delta_2^1$-variant, and this discrepancy persists in the
context of closed unbounded measures.

Recent breakthroughs in Natural Language Understanding have been driven by the success of pre-trained language models. However, the challenge of fine-tuning these models for new tasks and domains continues to be a significant hurdle. This paper proposes a novel solution, dubbed "Adapter", which enables the effective transfer of knowledge from a source to a target language model. By introducing an innovative "adapter" structure that is tailored to specific objectives, our approach enables models to be adapted for tasks such as sentiment classification, question answering, and machine translation. In contrast to existing methods, our solution is capable of fully leveraging the knowledge acquired by the adapters, resulting in substantial improvements in performance on a range of tasks. This breakthrough is highlighted by empirical evidence demonstrating that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art results by a significant margin, including a 4.0% improvement in SOTA on the SNLI dataset and a 4.3% improvement on the SemEval-2017 Task 5 benchmark for sentiment classification.

The global database of traffic signs on the Mapillary platform has reached a significant size, comprising of over a million images from diverse countries. Our research leverages this dataset to explore traffic sign detection and classification, leveraging its massive scale and international coverage. We employ a sophisticated deep neural network architecture to tackle two key challenges: identifying and categorizing traffic signs globally. Our approach involves a dual-stream network that synergizes with advanced post-processing techniques to accurately classify traffic signs. We rigorously evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed methods, achieving exceptional performance on the newly created dataset from Mapillary.

Traditional collaborative filtering methods rely heavily on training data but struggle when faced with sparse and noisy data, thus seeking self-supervised learning techniques to enhance data representation. Researchers have introduced methods like autoencoders and contrastive learning to improve user-item interactions. However, these approaches often require tailored designs, which can be challenging to implement. This paper proposes SelfCF, a self-supervised learning framework built around cooperative filtering, capable of harnessing diverse information within training data to improve user-item interactions. Through experiments on two real-world datasets, the study demonstrates SelfCF's effectiveness in improving recommendation accuracy.

We have established a new class of invariant measures for $\mathbb{P}^1$ with specific characteristics by extending existing definitions based on Tevelev levels. These new measures, referred to as generalized Tevelev levels, are based on a class of affine line maps that preserve a measure $\mu$ and result in a measure with the same property. The generalized Tevelev levels are included in the class of Tonelli-Carleman measures and share similar invariance properties under the action of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{R})$.

A novel gapped Dirac semimetal phase is proposed, featuring linearly-intersecting bands with parabolic dispersions at its critical point, which we identify as a Dirac point. By examining the low-energy behavior of this gapped Dirac semmadel phase, we establish that the surface state fermion spectrum follows a parabolic dispersion pattern, resulting in a circular Fermi surface at the Fermi level. Furthermore, our study reveals that the predicted gapped Dirac semmadel phase is experimentally detectable through measurements of the quantum oscillation.

We investigate the holonomy map near a gentle arc in the 2-disk bending problem and find that it maps to a subset of the 2-sphere, specifically an arc of constant length. By examining this arc and its associated problem of finding inscribed convex shapes, we develop an entry-exit map and prove its differentiability using the Birkhoff fixed-point theorem.

The current understanding of gravitational waves is centered on second-order modes, with third-order modes remaining a relatively unexplored area of research. In this study, we investigate the detectability of gravitational third-order modes, with a focus on their emergence due to the effects of cosmological acceleration. Our findings indicate that third-generation detectors may be able to detect these modes, with their detectability being feasible under certain conditions. In particular, we demonstrate that third-order modes could be detectable in the presence of a cosmological acceleration-induced boost, even when this effect is relatively weak. Furthermore, we observe that third-order modes generated by the acceleration-enhanced effect are distinct from those produced by the standard second-order modes, with this distinctiveness being a consequence of the linearity of the perturbed Friedmann equation. In contrast, we find that third-order modes that arise from the effects of a non-accelerated universe are equivalent to their second-order counterparts, with this equivalence being a consequence of the linearity of the perturbed Friedmann equation.

Astronomers have been fascinated by eclipsing binaries for a long time, and recent breakthroughs in astrometry have allowed them to study many of these systems in greater detail. This article focuses on a specific type of eclipsing binary known as the partial-orbit binary, characterized by close proximity between the stars and relatively short orbital periods. Due to the proximity of these systems, their light curves are often severely disrupted by the complex interplay of shadows on the stars. This has made it difficult to derive accurate models of their light curves in the past. This study presents a new method for determining the parameters of partial-orbit binaries using Gaia astrometry, which can provide crucial information about the orbital motion of these systems. By combining this data with spectroscopic orbits, researchers can now obtain highly accurate measurements of the binary's mass ratio, even in cases where the light curve is severely compromised. This approach has been applied to the binary star system V471 Ara, resulting in a new estimate of its mass ratio and mass ratio uncertainties. This study demonstrates that astrometry can be a valuable tool for studying partial-orbit binaries, and it has the potential to provide accurate mass estimates for many other systems in the future.

This study aims to establish a correlation between crossover modes and selection methods in genetic algorithms to enhance the 0/1 Knapsack problem's solution. To achieve this, we explored a range of crossover modes and selection methods with the primary goal of evaluating their impact on genetic algorithm convergence. We investigate the effects of different crossover modes on the convergence speed, using a variety of evaluation metrics, such as the number of iterations, genetic diversity, dominance diversity, and Inertia weight. We also examine the influence of selection methods on convergence, focusing on the use of 1/2 random selection and 2-tournament selection. We introduce a novel genetic operator, the "1/2-2-tournament" crossover, which combines the benefits of 1/2 random and 2-tournament selection methods. We evaluate this operator alongside other crossover modes, including single, boundary, and uniform crossover, to assess their impact on convergence. Our results reveal that the "1/2-2-tournament" crossover mode outperforms the other modes, achieving the fastest convergence.

This research paper focuses on establishing $L^2$ estimates for a specific type of oscillatory integrals with three functions involved, also known as trilinear oscillatory integrals or TIOs. These TIOs appear in the spectral expansion of propagators for pseudodifferential operators. We demonstrate that for TIOs of convolution type, where the oscillatory integrals depend on the differences between variables, we can obtain sharp $L^2$ decay rates, which is more precise than the traditional $L^3$ estimates. This improvement in estimates will be useful in the study of time-frequency analysis and the non-stationary Fourier transform.

Discriminatory speech in social media poses a significant issue, primarily because existing detection tools are not effective in identifying such toxic language, and there is a lack of available training data. We propose a new approach that utilizes fine-tuned T5 models, trained with a combination of human-annotated and machine-generated datasets, to improve detection accuracy. Additionally, our research involves the creation of a new English multilingual coalition dataset, aligned with the standards of the NIST Multilingual Test Suite, to facilitate the evaluation of language models across multiple languages. The English coalition dataset consists of 10,000 examples, while other languages have fewer examples due to data scarcity. We compare our approach with the DASTR tool, a state-of-the-art system for detecting discriminatory language, and find that our proposed model significantly outperforms DASTR across all languages.

A novel approach to achieving interaction scaling through Quantum Monte Carlo is proposed. By utilizing QMC to solve the quantum two-electron Schrödinger equation, the concept of scaling interactions in quantum chemistry can be redefined. The idea is demonstrated by applying QMC to the He-He interaction problem. The resulting He-He interaction potential and scaling properties are analyzed using a model based on the Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian.

The 2020 US Presidential Election saw a significant increase in false claims about election integrity, with the President and other high-ranking officials repeatedly spreading baseless allegations of voter fraud. Despite this, the public lacked concrete evidence to disprove these assertions, leaving many people uncertain about the election's legitimacy. Social media played a significant role in disseminating these claims, with Twitter being particularly problematic due to its ease of use and widespread adoption. To combat this issue, our research team has developed a dataset of over 298,000 labeled tweets related to voter fraud, collected between June 1st and November 8th, 2020. Our data includes both supportive and opposing claims of voter fraud, along with neutral statements, to facilitate further research into automated election misinformation detection.

We investigate generic vector field transformations on compact, real $n$-dimensional manifolds, and on specific subsets of such transformations, demonstrate that for average Lyapunov exponents exceeding 0, the properties of SRB measures emerge, including their existence, distinctiveness, invariance under the transformation, and possessing continuous, mixing properties.

Recent breakthroughs in Deep Learning have led to the development of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) that can quantify the uncertainty of their predictions. This paper presents a novel approach, inspired by the concept of the "backtracking" algorithm, to encode the posterior distribution of BNNs. Unlike previous methods, our approach does not rely on approximations, instead, it leverages the posterior distribution to trace back to the predictive distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by showcasing its ability to enhance the performance of BNNs within a classification framework, as confirmed by our experiments.

The instanton method has been successfully applied in a wide range of quantum mechanical problems, such as calculating quantum tunneling effects in various physical systems. Notably, this approach has also been applied to estimate non-adiabatic transfer rates in molecular systems. While the instanton method has been applied to estimate this rate for over three decades, a recent paper has demonstrated that it can be used to derive a general expression for this rate in a simple model system, even in the presence of an infinite external force. The derived expression matches a widely accepted theory known as the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory. This comparison highlights the applicability of the instanton approach to estimate molecular transfer rates.

This research introduces an innovative method for managing pathways in petri nets, applying it to a specific class of structured petri nets, known as PM nets, to optimize the resolution of don't care conditions and streamline the synthesis of controllable petri nets from PM nets, thus enabling the creation of controlled petri nets that can steer PM nets towards desired states.

A theoretical analysis of the impact of thermoelectric properties in thin, layered alloys has been developed using a spin-based mechanism known as magnon drag. This impact is influenced by spin-orbit interactions and results in the generation of spin-polarized charge carriers through spin-to-charge conversion. Our developed theory is applied to a specific alloy, Heusler alloy Mn$_{2}$Au, to study its thermoelectric behavior. Our calculations show that the influence of spin-orbit interactions on the alloy's electronic structure is significant and can generate spin-polarized charge carriers. As a result, the alloy exhibits exceptionally high thermoelectric performance, specifically a spin signal of up to 10^7 V/W. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions of thermopower and figure of merit for the alloy are in agreement with experimental results and show potential for significant improvements.

This paper introduces a stochastic approach for the sum problem, building on previous work related to ideal generation and circulant matrix generation. A novel algorithm is presented, which relies on the fast Fourier transform to achieve efficiency. Notably, experimental findings demonstrate that the stochastic method rivals the performance of the fastest existing algorithms.

In 1974, McEliece posed an open question regarding irreducible polynomials of specific types over finite fields, which has since remained unanswered. This paper provides a proof of one of the key conjectures, specifically for polynomials of degree d, which when evaluated at elements of a finite field or its powerset, yield a non-zero result. Initially, the approach presented involves the use of components of elevated order and a counting principle. However, this yields a more restrictive finding than that originally sought by McEliece. An alternative method is then introduced, which demonstrates that the initial approach was indeed less optimal.

The UPPAAL verification tool is renowned for its capabilities in examining concurrent systems by modeling them as graphical graphs. Although graphical models are ideal for many systems, many more complex software applications are typically represented using text-based code. This study investigates the possibility of converting software code into a format utilizing WRL, UPPAAL's language, thereby enabling the application of UPPAAL's analysis tools. A new tool, REWRL, has been developed to automatically translate a wide range of OOP code, specifically Java, C, and Mercurial into UPPAAL's WRL language, with the goal of enabling UPPAAL's online tools for verifying the time-sensitive behavior of software programs.

A new, advanced imaging technique, known as imaging with compressed acquisition (ICA), uses a combination of a metamaterial panel and a compressive sensing algorithm to take two-dimensional images at a rapid pace, requiring only a few measurements each time. To make ICA more practical, we have developed a method to enhance the performance of the metamaterial panel by incorporating an end-to-end processing pipeline. This processing pipeline involves a forward model, a nonlinear optimization algorithm, and a compressive sensing reconstruction algorithm. Our approach is effective in improving the contrast and resolution of the images taken by ICA, even in the presence of noise. We have tested our method by analyzing images of a standard test image both numerically and experimentally, demonstrating its success.

The behavior of a hydrogen atom within a combined linearly polarized, counter-rotating laser field is simulated using time-dependent, non-relativistic quantum mechanics. This simulation involves a combination of two circularly polarized lasers interacting with a hydrogen atom, where one polarizes the electron in the x-y plane and the other aligns it with the z-axis. A differential Larmor current is generated between the electron and proton due to the orthogonal fields, resulting in a current-induced electromagnetic interaction. This interaction causes an energy shift equivalent to a current-dependent Stark shift, with an ac-Stark map illustrating the varying energy levels.

Image manipulation techniques have advanced, allowing for the creation of visually striking graphics, but these often lack authenticity and are easily detectable. We developed an innovative method to integrate text into images by leveraging deep neural networks that process visual and semantic cues. Our approach trains a generative model to convert a written phrase into an image while exchanging associated concepts between two input texts. For instance, when given the phrase "New York and Paris", the model generates an image representing the Statue of Liberty and the Eiffel Tower in an urban backdrop. We tested our method on both textual inputs and semantic maps of images to assess its ability to produce high-quality blended images. We evaluated its performance against state-of-the-art image manipulation techniques and human benchmarks.

The intricate process of gene expression involves a combination of fluctuations and precise control measures. As a result, the study of RNA molecules exhibits irregular paths of production and destruction over time. To analyze these paths, we have developed a statistical framework that can extract various types of information, such as the average production rate, the standard deviation of production and destruction events, and the duration between events. This framework is flexible and can accommodate different types of data, including those with or without time information, and even simulated numerical data. Furthermore, we have demonstrated its effectiveness in uncovering new information about the transcriptional dynamics of E. coli's ribosomal protein Rps13, such as the presence of correlations between production rates and time intervals.

In education, data analysis is a crucial component of effective large-scale teaching, yet current educational research mainly focuses on quantitative methods for gathering data. This research aims to develop a qualitative approach to data analysis that can be used to inform empirical education research. By analyzing quotes from student interviews, we applied a qualitative analysis technique to a corpus of data. However, we found that this traditional approach is impractical for large datasets due to its time-consuming nature and the risk of researchers being influenced by the data. Therefore, we propose a model that can automatically identify key quotes and allow researchers to review findings, minimize bias, and interact with the findings to refine the model. This interaction can be facilitated through various visualizations that provide different perspectives on the data. By combining qualitative and quantitative methods, we can derive a measure of quote importance and validate our findings using student survey data. Our results show that this hybrid approach can be a useful tool for researchers, educators, and students, and we provide a roadmap for future research to further develop and refine this methodology.

The training process in layer-wise Quantum Approximate Optimization (QAOA) can be likened to an optimization problem, where determining the optimal method of optimization itself constitutes an even more complex issue. This intricate relationship may lead to an overemphasis on optimizing the training to the detriment of the quality of the mappable parameters, thereby impairing the algorithm's overall efficacy. This study delves into the effects of the training optimization on the results of QAOA, with a focus on optimizing the gradient of the QAOA parameter.

As the prevalence of multimedia social services, like online healthcare systems, grows, so does the potential for sensitive medical data to be compromised. Protecting the confidentiality of these systems is now a top priority, and safeguarding patient information from identification in shared datasets is a key objective. In this study, we tackle the challenge of protecting patient data by developing an algorithm that ensures individual anonymity. Our approach is rooted in previous research by the authors, and it's designed to address problems arising in the re-identification process, including data imperfections and varying feature numbers. Additionally, we've created a comprehensive dataset consisting of 20,000 samples with 40 attributes, and our method has been tested on this dataset to validate its effectiveness.

Time series data is widely used in the energy sector, particularly in the power system sector, where it plays a crucial role in analyzing and managing the power grid. However, this type of data is susceptible to data quality issues, particularly in the power sector, resulting from the increasing reliance on smart grid technologies. These issues pose significant challenges to accurately modeling and simulating power system dynamics. This study proposes a new method for handling missing data in time series that leverages the patterns and correlations within data, rather than relying on assumptions. The proposed method is particularly beneficial for the power system sector as it is based on data patterns rather than assumed distributions. The proposed method is compared to traditional data imputation techniques and evaluated using multiple metrics. The evaluation reveals that the new method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and effectiveness.

We examine a method for solving the optimization problem, which is represented by min$_x \langle f, x \rangle$ subject to $x \in A$, where $A$ is defined as the solution set of an inclusion $0 \in TX(x)$. Here, $TX(x)$ denotes the subdifferential of a convex function $T: X \to (-\infty, +\infty]$ defined on a Banach space $X$. Our approach is built on a regularization technique and relies on a condition for the subsequence of solutions that are obtained. This condition is based on the sequence of norms of the subdifferentials of $T$ evaluated at the solutions. We demonstrate that this condition is sufficient for the convergence of the solutions to the sole solution of the optimization problem, which is the fixed point of the subdifferential $TX$. Additionally, we establish the rate of convergence of the sequence of iterates produced by the method.

We investigate the interior point set within the regular tetrahedron, which fulfills a unique geometric condition, forming a planar pattern when projected from the outside inward. This specific set serves as a connection between two significant mathematical concepts: the isoxial Fuchsian ensemble and the projective generalised Frobenius ganita and the isoxial planar grove. Utilising the properties of the tetrahedron's faces and their dual elements, known as face-centres and vertices, we derive an efficient method to identify all possible interior points. With this approach, we demonstrate that there are 86 specific geodesic crosspoints with this property within the regular tetrahedron, and we provide an alternative representation method for them.

The process of $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ is analyzed and its sensitivity to lepton flavor violation is examined. A subsequent two-body decay of $\Upsilon (3S)$ to $e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ and $e^{\pm}e^{\mp}$ is considered, revealing that the former decay is more susceptible to lepton flavor violation effects. Assuming a $c\bar{c}s\bar{c}$ final state, we calculate the cross-section for $e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ production at $\Upsilon (3S)$ and $\Upsilon (5S)$ energy levels. With the planned BEPCII upgrade, we find that the $e\mu$ forward backward asymmetry could reach a $10^{-6}$ or even $10^{-7}$ level, which is comparable to other two-fermion production methods.

The mechanism behind stress-enhanced superconductivity in flat-band systems is still not fully understood. Our study reveals that applying pressure to Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ increases its superconducting temperature significantly. Interestingly, this effect scales with the amount of pressure applied and the composition of the material, but is unaffected by temperature changes, suggesting a non-linear relationship. Our findings are consistent with a theoretical model proposed by Kitaoka et al., which describes the interplay between linear and quadratic components of pressure's effect on superconductivity.

We have developed a method to extract black hole data from the event horizon using available thermodynamic data in four-dimensional JT gravity. By applying this method, we can accurately calculate the Page curve, confirming it matches previously derived results. Additionally, we have utilized this method to determine the full time evolution of a black hole's geometry, thermodynamics, and entanglement structure. To achieve this, we first converted given thermodynamic data into corresponding data for bulk geometry and Hawking radiation modes. Then, we integrated the modes according to their principal values, which are directly related to their mutual entanglement. The resulting time evolution reflected the complexities of the horizon's Page time and entropies. The data allowed us to extract the time-dependent form of the metric and scalar field, as well as the full entanglement spectrum, which is essential for understanding the horizon's quantum behavior.

Neural ODEs have been found to outperform RNNs in sequential learning tasks, but their effectiveness relies on having continuous, low-error input measurements. In contrast, real-world sequential data often involves noisy observations prone to sudden spikes of high uncertainty. To address this limitation, we introduce Neural SDEs, a class of models that can learn with input sequences featuring high variability and non-repeating noise patterns. Key to our approach is treating input data as a random process and using a deep latent process to learn the underlying SDE, which we encode using neural networks. Our method is shown to be interpretable, efficient, and capable of handling complex tasks such as image and text prediction, even with input sequences featuring sudden, large changes.

The objective of object-target navigation is to guide an agent to a specific target object within a cluttered environment, identified through a single observation image. We propose a innovative navigation approach, the Object Recall Transformer, which is designed to effectively recall previously seen objects and adapt to changing scenes. Unlike conventional object-target navigation methods, our approach employs a recall-based strategy to identify and adapt to unseen objects and targets, leveraging a multi-image training framework to simulate this behavior. By training the model to predict actions and predict object characteristics based on a sequence of images, we demonstrate improved performance and generalization capabilities. We also provide a detailed analysis of the model's performance and recall strategies.

Current approaches to fine-tuning pre-trained language models for task-agnostic instruction following have limitations in generalizing to unseen task categories due to their reliance on task-specific training data. This paper introduces a novel fine-tuning method, dubbed OPT-IML, which leverages pre-training data from the 175 billion token OPT model to enhance low-resource instruction following tasks. By utilizing the pre-trained OPT model as a base model and developing a novel meta-learning algorithm, our approach significantly enhances generalization to novel task categories. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by 2.2-5.9 absolute points on the SuperGLUE benchmark across various under-resourced languages in multilingual settings.

The open source programming environment Scratch has gained popularity due to its user-friendly interface, especially attracting young users through its intuitive design. Although numerous studies have analyzed the demographics of Scratch users, there is a lack of research on the diverse path that users take to achieve their goals in Scratch. This study aims to fill this gap by employing a network analysis of Scratch users' interactions to explore the concept of peripheral participation, where users engage with the community in various ways. Our research examines the extent of peripheral participation on Scratch, highlighting the diverse nature of contributors and their activities. This study also investigates the relationship between peripheral participation, user goals, and demographic factors. Our findings suggest that users participate in Scratch in a multifaceted manner, and that the complexity of their activities is influenced by their objectives and age.

A transcorrelated electron gas is examined in the context of a homogeneous electron gas at thermal equilibrium. We use a method based on resolving the Schrödinger equation to determine the ground and excited states of the gas, as well as the response of the system to an external electric field. The electron-electron interaction is transformed into a simpler correlation J that depends only on the relative positions of the electrons. The resulting transcorrelated Hamiltonian system is then solved to determine the system's properties. The accuracy of the method is evaluated by comparing the results to those obtained using the random phase approximation, and the method is also applied to study the response of the gas to a periodic potential. The findings are compared with available numerical data.

We suggest a constrained covariance augmentation method to incorporate physical knowledge, referred to as physically restricted covariance augmentation (PRCA). This approach can be applied in various scenarios, such as integrating wheel position information in autonomous driving or the movement of one or multiple legs in mobile robots. The method is based on a joint distribution of wheel/leg positions and has a lower computational cost than full covariance matrices. To handle high-dimensional position uncertainty, a simplified Gaussian process is employed to model the correlation function and approximate the covariance function via an optimal transportation problem. An alternative method is also presented to reduce computational requirements. The proposed method is then compared to random covariance matrices on a virtual autonomous vehicle simulation and demonstrates comparable accuracy under certain conditions while offering improved computational efficiency.

In the context of massive datasets, ensuring data security and confidentiality presents significant challenges, largely due to the substantial storage and processing demands of the most effective encryption methods. To address this issue, this study introduces a pioneering solution for safeguarding large datasets, utilizing an optimized algorithm for decomposing complex network structures into smaller, manageable parts. By employing this algorithm, it's possible to break down a massive tensor into a group of smaller tensors, enabling a distributed computing approach that's particularly beneficial for distributed memory-based systems. Furthermore, this study presents a novel method for randomly selecting users and calculating partial tensor values in a probabilistic manner, thus minimizing data replication and reducing data processing time. Experimental results demonstrate the superior efficiency and performance of this proposed solution, making it an ideal choice for large datasets that require secure processing.

Transferring learning-based robot control policies from simulation to reality is hindered by the challenge of ensuring safety during the simulation-to-real process. A proposed solution involves a learning agent utilizing a diverse range of policies learned from multiple simulated training environments with varying levels of difficulty. This safety-by-variability approach is demonstrated to be effective in both offline and online settings, where it successfully transfers a quadruped robot's balancing skill from simulation to reality without encountering obstacles.

The presence of jet activity in various astrophysical sources, encompassing radio galaxies and quasars at all cosmic distances, is a long-standing phenomenon that has garnered substantial interest. Although these objects share a radio emission signature, their physical nature and radio morphology can vary significantly. Observations of nearby AGN have revealed intricate jet structures, with the recent detection of relativistic jets in GRBs at great distances. This review will examine radio jets in galaxies and quasars through a theoretical and experimental approach, exploring their evolution in recent years. The discovery of intricate jet structures, coupled with improved observational capabilities, has provided valuable insights into the nature of these objects. Theoretical advancements have also allowed us to better comprehend their behavior, which is particularly relevant in explaining the diverse radio emission patterns observed in GRB afterglows.

This research focuses on real-time estimation of time-nonstationary, nonlinear autoregressive processes using concurrent methods. The non-linear processes are modelled using Fuzzy Cellular Automata, a novel approach to complex dynamics. Two concurrent estimation frameworks are explored and their performance evaluated against a standard algorithmic estimator. The study utilises a simulated dataset of the US Consumer Price Index to compare the efficacy of these techniques.

This research aims to develop the first open-source language identification frameworks that can process real-time text inputs. Two novel neural network architectures are proposed, designed to predict whether a message is aggressive or not. Our models were trained on a dataset of over 200,000 English-language tweets and tested on the CAID dataset to evaluate their performance. While they demonstrate strong predictive capabilities, the models still make errors, particularly when it comes to predicting aggression in less common languages. To address this limitation, we created a bi-directional neural network that can provide more confident predictions. This new model was trained and tested on the CAID dataset and showed improved predictive confidence while maintaining a strong accuracy rate.

The brain's various regions interact with each other through a complex network of interactions. Unfortunately, current methods for mapping these connections rely heavily on limited experiments that only scratch the surface of the brain's true connectivity. As a result, we need new approaches to uncover the underlying network structure using large amounts of simulated data. We've developed a novel artificial intelligence-based method to study the brain's functional network by simulating the activity of thousands of brain regions. This approach identifies the most important connections that help us understand how different brain regions interact with each other. By analyzing simulated data, we've found that brain regions that work together during certain tasks tend to have stronger connections with each other. We've also discovered that brain regions that are close together in the brain tend to have stronger connections with each other.

This work investigates a time-varying system comprising a linear operator, a quadratic function, and a random perturbation, with a focus on the convergence of an algorithm inspired by Nesterov, utilizing a technique similar to the one enhanced by Chen et al. Building on the principles of a dissipative system, an enhanced version of the Nesterov algorithm can be formulated. A critical analysis of the algorithm's behavior yields two distinct outcomes: one indicating that the system's Lyapunov function decays exponentially, much like a standard exponentially stable system; the other suggests Lyapunov stability, akin to the behavior of a stable system. Furthermore, it is shown that the constant associated with the Lyapunov function may be minimized by optimizing a specific parameter. A numerical example is presented to validate the findings.

This study develops an implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta method to solve hyperbolic systems, particularly focusing on its performance in models with strong non-linear source terms such as the inviscid Burgers equation. By leveraging the structure of these systems, the method is efficiently implemented with a simple upwind operation on the boundary. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of two low-order upwind operations on the method's performance and discover that a single explicit step can be executed in a boundary cell without needing an implicit solution. Additionally, we find that this method exhibits high-order convergence and a high degree of stability in the $\alpha$-stable region, as well as efficient upwind operations in the system's space-time framework.

To increase the efficiency of solar cells in thin and ultrathin silicon and new materials, we have investigated the absorption enhancement capabilities of periodic 3D photonic band gap back reflectors in optical simulations. The reflectors were designed to work in the visible and near-infrared range, where silicon absorption peaks, and were effective in this range, achieving absorption rates of 85% in 200 nm and 90% in 50 nm silicon thickness. The high absorption rates in ultrathin silicon were attributed to the ability of the back reflectors to redirect light rays and increase the effective path length. The design of the back reflectors was also resistant to imperfections in ultrathin silicon layers. The results of this research have implications for other applications, such as photovoltaic boosters, sensors, and optical filters.

In cases where machine learning systems must make decisions under uncertain or ambiguous data, credal assessment networks can be applied to provide a probability distribution over possible world states. This study presents and evaluates credal assessment network learning algorithms, testing them on real-world data sets to compare their performance with established models from the field of probabilistic graphical models. The findings indicate that credal assessment networks can offer a more cautious approach in prediction compared to traditional probabilistic graphical models, while still maintaining similar levels of accuracy.

The task of K suggestion involves presenting the top-K results from a database in the correct order, prioritizing the most relevant items over less relevant ones. Prior research focused on learning a ranking function that scores items based on their relevance. However, this approach is flawed because it doesn't account for items tied in relevance, which can lead to incorrect suggestions (e.g. suggesting "car" over "car insurance" instead of starting with the latter). This paper introduces a new method, called probabilistic distance learning, which uses the distance between items to evaluate their relative relevance. It incorporates a new margin parameter that controls how far the top-K results can be from the top-ranked item in the result list. The method is also optimized to minimize the cost of the top-K results with the aid of a proxy metric. The experiments show that the proposed technique outperforms existing methods in several benchmarks, including the MS MARCO and TREC CAR datasets.

We investigate the ongoing non-Markovian behavior of quantum channels that do not lose their pure state to eliminate non-reversibility. Our analysis reveals that certain quantum channels exhibit a difference in the evolution of pure and mixed states, where this difference is a crucial indicator of non-Movarian dynamics. We utilize this concept to create two original definitions of non-Movarian quantum channels, which are based on the properties of pure and mixed states. Our research shows that these definitions are equivalent to other established methods for quantifying non-Movarian quantum channels. Our research also demonstrates that unital and trace-preserving quantum channels do not exhibit this type of non-Movarian dynamics.

The widespread use of machine learning algorithms in critical decision-making systems is a concern due to the lack of transparency in their complex models. In response, we developed an innovative method combining counterfactual inference and engaged learning to create more transparent AI. By utilizing a causal classifier, our proposed method provides users with deeper insights into predictions, reducing the risk of errors and misunderstandings. A case study on a real-world medical dataset reveals that our proposed method not only outperforms conventional approaches but also offers users a more in-depth understanding of predictions, thereby enhancing trust in AI systems.

The primary goal of a robot's environment map is to convey spatial relationships, enabling it to safely coexist with other agents. To achieve this goal, various approaches have been developed, often combining point cloud data and high-definition maps. However, accurately comparing different methods remains a challenge due to their distinct application domains. To address this issue, we present RoSmEEry, a cutting-edge framework that simulates an environment for robots. This framework can be utilized to evaluate the performance of various semantic mapping techniques. By doing so, we aim to advance the field of research in semantic mapping and ultimately contribute to the growth of autonomous robots.

Rikudo is an online Japanese word game where players rearrange a set of seven lettered tiles, comprising of basic letters and those with unique values, to achieve a minimum score based on the value of the highest tile on each line. The game's objective is to find the highest-scoring arrangement using these tiles. In this study, we demonstrate that Rikudo is an NP-complete problem by developing a polynomial-time reduction from the Exact Cover by 3-sets problem.

This document outlines a collection of cutting-edge computational methods developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) for modeling complex transportation networks. These methods enable accurate and efficient simulation of traffic flow on networks, even with vast amounts of data, allowing for timely and precise predictions. A key innovation at NIST is the implementation of a highly scalable algorithm for network flow, which can seamlessly integrate with a range of transportation modeling frameworks.

Ramanujan introduced several key identities connected to theta functions and the theta and Jacobi theta series, denoted by θ(x), θ1(x), θ3(x), θ4(x), and ϑ(x), respectively. We present a new interpretation of his modular formulas for theta functions, and using this framework, we organize the identities in a block-form through Hecke relations. We also discover that Hecke operators can simplify Ramanujan's modular formulas for Jacobi theta functions, leading to a new, coarser organization of these identities.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of eight gravitationally lensing quasars, utilizing a unique dataset of Hubble Space Telescope F160W photometry and Keck ESI spectroscopy. By leveraging these observations, we've been able to derive accurate redshifts and dispersion measurements for the lensing galaxies, along with photometric redshifts and structural parameters for the quasars. Furthermore, we've applied a novel lens model fitting technique to each system, yielding precise mass-to-light estimates for the quasars.
